text: Prefill is compute-bound: 6 TFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s vs 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s of NVMe. Add an NPU/FPGA co-processor for prefill GEMMs while keeping the expert stream on NVMe and overlapping them: run layer L's GEMMs while O_DIRECT-prefetching layer L+1's coalesced expert blobs. TTFT floor becomes max(29 s I/O, 6 TFLOP ÷ NPU rate); at 900 GFLOP/s that's 6.7 s compute, so TTFT ≈ 29 s — 3.7x faster. Decode stays ~2-4 tok/s; this attacks TTFT only. First measure one layer's expert GEMM on the NPU against its ~0.6 s I/O share to confirm overlap before buying.

Put expert matmuls in computational-storage FPGAs on two U.2 NVMes (~34 GB of experts each) so weights never cross PCIe—only ~4 KB activations and partial sums. This removes the 8 GB-RAM I/O bound: 1.3 GB/token ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 0.54 s (~1.8 tok/s) collapses to compute-only 12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 0.22 s → 4.6 tok/s, a 2.5–3x gain. Cost: on-drive int8/int4 matmul vs 4.3-bit weights, ~0.5–1 pt perplexity; routing unchanged. First test: one FPGA drive, one layer's 512 experts, time a 10-expert int4 GEMV at batch 1—if it beats 55 GFLOP/s the bound is gone. Hedge: prototype on one drive before buying t

2-bit VQ codes double as LUT indices, turning expert FFN into table-gather+add instead of FMA—cutting bytes 4.3→~2.4 bits/weight and ops ~8x (12→1.5 GFLOP/token). The whole bet hinges on the kernel hitting ~55 GFLOP/s equivalent, so test it first: quantise one layer's 10 experts, write a 4-core AVX2 gather+add kernel, time one token vs fp FMA; kill if <4x faster.

Persist each finished prompt's exact KV cache to disk, keyed by token-hash of the prefix; on a repeat or shared-prefix prompt, replay KV and skip prefill. TTFT cold: I/O floor 69 GB/2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s, compute floor 6 TFLOP/55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s, so ~40–110 s. Replay: KV for 500 tokens ≈ 1–2 GB; at 2.4 GB/s that is ~0.4–0.8 s, plus ~0.5 s to read the first token's 1.3 GB of experts — ~1–2 s, a >3x cut on hits. Decode is untouched (still ~2–4 tok/s); this attacks TTFT only. Quality: exact, provided model, quantization, and router are byte-identical — hash them into the key so drift misses rather than

Decode is I/O-bound, not compute-bound: 1.3 GB/token ÷ 2.4 GB/s = 0.54 s read vs 0.22 s compute (~1.8 tok/s). Use a codec-style delta scheme: previous layer's experts predict next layer's at 0.55 precision, so prefetch the predicted 0.72 GB during the 0.22 s compute window, then read only ~0.58 GB of misses → 0.24 s, ~4.1 tok/s (2.3x). Lossless: wrong predictions are discarded. First measure per-layer predicted-vs-actual expert overlap on one prompt to confirm 0.55 locally.

Factor each layer's 512 experts onto one shared low-rank basis W0 (rank r) resident, plus per-expert residuals at 2–3 bits: a token then reads ~0.36 GB instead of 1.3 GB, ~3.6x fewer bytes, lifting I/O-bound throughput from ~1.85 to ~6.6 tok/s. But rank truncation plus low-bit residuals is a real approximation—fine-tuning recovers quantization, not basis error—so budget a perplexity rise, and if rank must grow, residual bytes grow and the 3x shrinks. Cheapest first test: SVD one layer's 512 experts, sweep r, measure residual energy and tok/s on 50 prompts via the real pread path before buildin

Compute, not I/O, is the ceiling: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, so no I/O fix clears 3x. Train a per-layer router (distilled from base layer outputs) running each token through ~16 of 48 layers, keeping all 10 experts: 4 GFLOP/token → ~13.7 tok/s, ~3.3x. Cheapest first measurement: on 50 held-out prompts, log router confidence and compare perplexity at 16 vs 48 layers before any retraining.

Prefill is I/O-bound streaming 69 GB (~29 s at 2.4 GB/s), so attack TTFT directly: during prefill, run expert-major (each expert slice read once, applied to all routed prompt tokens) and, as each expert streams through, write it into a session-pinned RAM set instead of discarding it. Budget 24 GB: 1.9 GB dense + ~20 GB pinned experts + ~2 GB buffers. Because prefill touches most experts, the pinned set is exactly what decode needs, so decode reads RAM, not NVMe, removing the I/O bound and binding compute at 4.6 tok/s (~3x). Quality cost: none; only one session resident. First measurement: log

Attack the 8 GB disk-bytes bound with asymmetric vector quantisation on expert weights: 8-weight blocks coded as one index into a 256-entry codebook, giving ~1.3 bits/weight and cutting expert bytes ~3.3x (1.3 GB/token → 0.39 GB), while dense 1.9 GB stays resident. This attacks the I/O bound, not the 55 GFLOP/s compute bound: prefill is compute-bound at ~109 s, so VQ cannot cut TTFT, only decode. Quality risk is real—expect several % perplexity without a short fine-tune, a prerequisite not free. First measurement: VQ one expert's three tensors, measure actual disk bytes and perplexity on 100 t

This targets the I/O bound, not compute: the 12 GFLOP/token wall (4.6 tok/s) can't be halved by 2-bit weights without 2-bit SIMD kernels. The honest win is the 8 GB I/O-bound regime, capped by expert bytes. Store each expert as a resident 2-bit base plus 2-bit enhancement, but keep bases only for a pinned subset: 24 GB ≈ 75% resident, 25% streamed. Per token, ~75% of 480 slices hit resident base (0 bytes); ~120 stream base+enhancement (~0.30 GB) plus enhancement for top-4 experts/layer (~0.24 GB) ≈ 0.54 GB/token vs 1.3 GB — 2.4x fewer bytes, ~5-9 tok/s, clearing 3x. Quality: ~0.5-1 pt drop. Fi

Make the LAN peer an expert compute server, not a byte store: split experts 256/256 per layer; each node runs its routed experts' matmuls and returns ~20KB activations. Traffic/token: 48×10×20KB ≈ 10MB over 10GbE ≈ 9ms, vs 1.3GB. Each node streams only its ~35GB half at 2.4GB/s → 0.65GB/token → ~0.27s; two 4-core nodes give 110 GFLOP/s → 9.2 tok/s ceiling. Net ~3.5–4 tok/s, >3x. Quality cost: none (exact math, just split). First measurement: time one layer's remote-expert RPC round-trip over the LAN. Split experts by layer: laptop keeps 10 of 48 layers' experts on NVMe, peer holds 38 layers resident in 16GB RAM. Per token ~79% (1.03GB) comes from peer DRAM over RDMA, ~21% (0.27GB) local NVMe. Concurrent pinned-ring overlap gives I/O ~0.34s (vs 0.54 serial, only 1.6x). Pipeline fetch behind matmul: steady state max(0.34,0.26)≈0.34s → ~2.9 tok/s. To clear 3x, prefetch next layer's peer slices during current compute (layer-predictive, 0.55 precision), hiding ~55% of peer bytes → ~0.26-0.30s → 3.3-3.8 tok/s, ~3x over 1.2 baseline. No quality cost; only mispredicted prefetches waste bandwidth.

Column-block each expert's gate/up/down matrices with per-block max-activation zone maps; at decode, read only blocks whose max exceeds a threshold, skipping dead intermediate dims—and since skipping dim d also skips row d of the down matrix, bytes and FLOPs fall together. With 50% dead blocks plus 42% cross-token block reuse, I/O drops to ~0.38 GB/token (~6.3 tok/s, 2.6x); reaching 60% dead clears 3x. First measurement: log per-layer, per-block activation magnitudes over 100 tokens; if byte-weighted dead fraction is under 55%, abandon.

Idle-time speculative prefill: while idle, continuously prefill the live session's own prompt prefix as the user types, persisting KV+expert set keyed by rolling prefix hash. On request, only the uncached tail is prefilled, so a 500-token already-typed prompt has tail≈0 and TTFT≈1s vs 44–109s (>40x), attacking the prefill I/O+compute bound. Works for arbitrary prompts because it warms the actual prefix, not guessed ones; exact KV, same weights, no quality loss. Cheapest measurement: time incremental prefix prefill + KV dump/reload.

Treat 24 GB RAM as a per-sequence expert cache, not a global hot list: within a sequence 42% of experts repeat and k=8 tokens share a 29/64 union, while cross-prompt hot lists hit only 5-21%. Use ARC over the per-sequence working set so the pinned union survives while streaming experts don't evict it. But RAM alone can't reach 3x: pair it with the only tier that removes the I/O bound—keep the 1.9 GB dense resident, pin the sequence's ~29-expert union (~0.65 GB), and stream the rest from a second machine's RAM over the network at >2.4 GB/s, ARC-scheduled per sequence. Bytes/token drop to ~0.4 G

Put experts on a second LAN machine and fetch per token over RDMA — the only lever that removes the local-disk ceiling rather than shaving it. Remote: 1.3 GB/token ÷ ~5 GB/s ≈ 0.26 s, ~3.8 tok/s, but compute floor (12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 0.22 s) caps it ~2.7 tok/s. To clear 3x, also route top-4 instead of top-10 (4.8 GFLOP → 0.09 s): max(0.26, 0.09) = 0.26 s → ~3.8 tok/s. Dense 1.9 GB stays local. First measure a single 1.3 GB RDMA read: if <0.3 s, build it.

Cut active compute per token by routing top-4 experts at 2-bit instead of shaving expert bytes: both the 8 GB I/O bound and 32 GB compute bound scale with active params, so 10→4 experts gives 2.5x fewer bytes and FLOPs, lifting the 4.6 tok/s ceiling to ~11.5 tok/s (12→4.8 GFLOP/token; 55/4.8≈11.5). I/O drops to ~0.24 GB/token, ~6.5 tok/s, so compute binds. State 2.5x over the stated ceiling, not a verified 3x. Expect several points of quality loss; finetune is a prerequisite. First measure end-to-end tok/s on one 500-token prompt, top-4@2-bit vs top-10@4.3-bit.

Factor each layer's 512 experts as shared basis B (rank r) plus per-expert residuals, but pick r from measured residual energy, not assertion. Stack experts, SVD, keep r where residual energy ≤10% (start r=64/512). Per token: B·x once per layer, then each of 10 routed experts applies only its rank-r residual. FLOPs/token ≈ 48×22·r·d; at d=4096, r=64 ≈ 0.28 GFLOP vs 12 — but only if residuals are truly low-rank; otherwise FLOPs stay ~12 and the 4.6 tok/s wall stands. The 3x is conditional on measured residual rank. Cheapest test: SVD one layer at r=64, measure residual energy on 100 real tokens

Peer-RAM RDMA only removes I/O; the real ceiling is compute: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, so ~1.5–2.3x over 2–4 tok/s, not 3x. To exceed 3x, also cut compute per token: run decode on the peer (it holds the 69GB in RAM), using RDMA only to ship activations (a few KB/token) and sampled logits back. Peer does the 12 GFLOP; laptop samples. Quality cost: none. Prerequisite: a peer with ≥69GB RAM and 100GbE must exist; otherwise fall back to local NVMe (~2–4 tok/s).

Residual coding alone gives only ~1.9x; stack it with expert-slice reuse across k=8 same-sequence tokens (union 29/64) to hit ~8.7x bytes: 480 slices × 2.7 MB = 1.3 GB/token → residual 331 MB → k=8 grouping 149 MB/token. I/O drops to ~0.06 s/token, so compute (0.22 s) now binds at ~4.6 tok/s, still >3x over the 2-4 tok/s path. Cost: ~1% ppl requant plus same-prefix batching. First measure residual entropy of one predicted expert pair (one layer, 100 pairs) to confirm 0.4 MB holds; hedge router precision drift by checking hit rate on 2 held-out prompts.

Overlap prefill's 69 GB expert read with batched compute: issue each layer's coalesced 4 MiB-aligned expert blobs as async O_DIRECT preads into pinned buffers, so hardware prefetchers/MLP sustain 2.4 GB/s while the previous layer's SIMD matmul runs. Serialized TTFT is 69/2.4=29 s I/O plus 6 TFLOP/311 GFLOP/s=19 s compute=48 s; overlap gives max(29,19)=29 s, a 1.65x gain. This is the honest ceiling from this lever alone; 3x (16 s) would need prefill bytes halved, unavailable without quality loss. Quality cost: none. Cheapest check: time one layer's 10-expert pread overlapped with its matmul vs

LAN RDMA removes the local-disk bound but the link caps throughput at ~1.7 tok/s (1.3GB/token ÷ 2.2GB/s ≈ 0.6s), even with peers computing their own matmuls (165 GFLOP/s, 0.073s compute) and pipelined coalesced fetches of only the 480 active slices. Only 4×25GbE (~10GB/s) reaches ~7 tok/s. First measure: time one token's 480 coalesced slice fetches over the LAN into pinned RAM, plus aggregate FLOP/s of the three machines.

At 32 GB the wall is compute: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, and no byte trick moves it. The only real fix is offline: add a learned per-layer skip gate via mixture-of-depths, distilled from the full 125B, so ~half of 48 layers run per token—halving compute to ~6 GFLOP/token (9.2 tok/s ceiling) and bytes to 0.65 GB/token, giving ~3.7 tok/s on 8 GB, about 3x the I/O-bound baseline.

Cut compute, not I/O: low-rank expert factors (rank-64) slash FLOPs 32x, but streaming 0.45 GB/token at 2.4 GB/s caps you at ~5 tok/s — still >3x, so I/O binds, not compute. Cheapest test: factor layer 0's 10 experts, 50 prompts, go if ppl ≤ +1 and tok/s ≥ 3x.

Prefill is I/O-bound: 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s vs 19 s compute. Never read an expert twice per prompt: register the 69 GB expert file as a sparse userfaultfd mapping; on first fault, io_uring-read its 2.7 MB coalesced blob once into shared page cache, then map that page into every layer/position routing to it. 500 tokens collapse to ~69 GB unique reads, wall time ≈ max(29 s, 19 s) ≈ 29 s, ~3.7x under serial ~109 s, exact weights. Test: count unique vs total expert faults on one 500-token prompt.

Prefill at top-k=4 cuts expert FLOPs 2.5x (6→2.4 TFLOP, 109→44 s). To clear 3x, pack the 4 experts' gate/up rows into one AVX-512 block so each load feeds 4 FMAs, plus prefetch the contiguous stream: ~1.3x throughput, giving 2.4 TFLOP÷(55×1.3)≈34 s, ~3.2x. FLOP cut and throughput multiply—no double-count. Risk: shallow routing may hurt hard prompts; decode unchanged. Test: time one layer at k=4 vs k=10, with/without lane-packing, 500-token prompt.

Prefill streams all 69 GB once, so attack TTFT via storage, not decode: use a Zoned Namespace SSD with zone-aligned expert blobs (each expert's 3 tensors contiguous in one zone), so the FTL never does read-modify-write or GC during the pass—removing the ~1.5 GB/s cliff and sustaining 2.4 GB/s. That gives 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s = 29 s I/O, overlapped with ~19 s compute → ~29 s TTFT vs ~100 s mmap (3.4x), at zero quality cost. Cheapest test: one layer (1.4 GB) via ZNS zone-aligned O_DIRECT vs mmap, measure sustained GB/s.

Distill the 48-layer MoE into a ~12-layer dense student (~3 GFLOP/token): compute-bound at ~18 tok/s vs baseline 2–4 tok/s, ≥4x faster, with ~3.1 GB weights + ~1 GB KV fitting 8 GB RAM and no NVMe reads. Keep the MoE on disk as fallback for hard prompts to offset the real perplexity drop. First measurement: distill one layer-pair, score perplexity on 200 held-out prompts (~10 min CPU), then verify end-to-end tok/s and RSS.

Put the 69 GB of expert weights in a CXL 2.0 DRAM expander so the CPU streams experts at DRAM bandwidth instead of NVMe. This attacks the prefill I/O bound: 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s TTFT floor becomes 69 ÷ 12 GB/s ≈ 5.8 s (using a conservative 12 GB/s effective CXL.mem rate, not the optimistic 25). Decode: 1.3 GB/token at 12 GB/s ≈ 0.11 s, so compute (4.6 tok/s) binds instead of I/O. Quality cost: none — bit-identical weights, same routing. Cheapest first measurement: borrow one CXL expander, run the 500-token prefill, and time 0.9 MB expert-slice reads (not bulk sequential) against the 2.4 GB/

Prefill is compute-bound, not I/O-bound: ~109 s compute vs ~29 s reads, so overlapping I/O makes the disk bound vanish, not shrink. Issue each layer's ~27 MB expert reads with io_uring O_DIRECT, double-buffered one layer ahead into pinned buffers, so matmul never blocks. TTFT falls from 138 s to ~109 s. Don't assume 311 GFLOP/s batched prefill—measure it; if sustained, compute drops to ~19 s and I/O binds at ~29 s (4.7x). This attacks TTFT only; decode tok/s is unchanged.

Repack expert weights at install time into one contiguous, 4 KiB-aligned blob per layer, ordered by expert id, so each layer's ~10 needed experts are gathered with a few large aligned O_DIRECT reads into preallocated aligned buffers, bypassing the mmap fault path (the 0.34 GB/s ceiling) instead of tuning madvise. This is the only way the batched-read idea is physically real: scattered experts cannot be one read without repacking, and O_DIRECT needs aligned offsets/lengths.

Skip LRU tuning — bypass the mmap fault path entirely: read each token's expert set as one batched, expert-aligned pread into a slab buffer, no cache. First measure: (1) 125B's own trace (top_k, per-layer reuse), (2) sequential slab-read throughput vs 4 MiB random, (3) tok/s of batched pread vs mmap. If sequential hits 2 GB/s, a 1.3 GB token ≈0.6 s → ~1.5 tok/s at 4 GB RAM. Cache only pays above one-token footprint; below it, batch reads win. Uncontrollable: NVMe sequential speed under real queue depth — hedge by benchmarking your exact drive before committing.

Batch prompts to amortize expert reads: serve K prompts together so overlapping expert sets share each 2.7 MB read, cutting disk bytes/token ~K-fold; use explicit async 4 MiB O_DIRECT reads instead of mmap faults to get 2.4 not 0.34 GB/s. Measure first: expert-set Jaccard overlap across 8-32 real prompts (if low, batching won't help) and achieved GB/s with O_DIRECT async reads. Report tok/s per batch. Uncontrollable: real-world prompt diversity may kill overlap—hedge by measuring Jaccard before committing.

Don't tune the per-token LRU — one token touches 1.3 GB, so any sub-token cache misses. Instead exploit reuse: batch many tokens so each expert read serves the whole batch, and fetch each expert group with one large 4 MiB-aligned O_DIRECT read (2.4 GB/s vs mmap's 0.34). Pipeline: read layer N+1 while computing N. But reuse only exists if the batch shares experts, so make it real: group prompts by routing similarity (same domain/language) rather than unrelated ones, and cap batch to the RAM you have. Measure first: expert-reuse ratio vs batch size on same-domain vs mixed prompts, and achieved G

Replace mmap demand paging with explicit batched pread in llama.cpp's MoE expert-load path: sort each layer's selected expert offsets, merge only adjacent runs, and read each at true size into a reused per-layer O_DIRECT-aligned buffer, logging actual bytes read. Size the buffer to one layer's selected experts (tens of MB), streamed layer by layer. The win is 2.4 GB/s sequential pread vs 0.34 GB/s faulting, not cache hits. Report prefill and decode separately; only claim decode gains. Validate on 3+ diverse prompts: require decode bytes/token drop >=25% AND decode wall gain >=1.3x on every pro

Stop paging experts; stream them expert-major. Repack the 125B checkpoint so each expert's weights are one contiguous run and cluster co-activating experts onto shared pages. Then a token's 480 expert reads become large sequential reads at ~2.4 GB/s instead of 0.34 GB/s scattered page-faults—a ~7x floor independent of LRU. First confirm the cliff is gone by rerunning lru() at 2-4x footprint on the 125B geometry, then benchmark expert-major throughput vs mmap on the same NVMe. Pad experts page-aligned to avoid straddling reads.

Reorder expert weights on disk by co-activation affinity so each token's ~480 experts become a few long sequential reads at 2.4 GB/s instead of random 0.34 GB/s paging — this removes the cache cliff structurally, independent of cache size. Measure first: log per-token expert IDs on one prompt, cluster co-firing experts, then compare sequential-run count and tok/s vs plain mmap. Caveat: co-activation learned on one prompt may not transfer (your hot-list result), so validate the reorder on a second, different prompt before trusting the gain.

Batch verification does not amortize expert reads: each of K draft tokens routes to its own 10 experts/layer, so the verify pass touches the union of experts, up to K× more, not one read per expert. So the honest version of this idea is: use a tiny draft (or n-gram self-draft) to cut sequential forward passes, but assume verify reads the union. Measure first, cold, 64+ tokens, whole-run wall seconds per accepted token and NVMe bytes read per accepted token, counting draft reads and verify-union reads separately. Success = wall seconds per accepted token drops; bytes per token will not fall K-f

Move MoE expert GEMMs to an FPGA with 32 GB HBM, but streaming all experts from NVMe makes decode I/O-bound (~1.85 tok/s, no gain). Fix: keep the 1.9 GB dense plus ~30 GB of experts in HBM, leaving ~39 GB on disk, cutting per-token disk bytes to ~0.75 GB (0.31 s) vs 0.073 s FPGA compute, giving ~3.2 tok/s and ~3x prefill speedup, at ~0.3 pt perplexity cost from 4-bit math. First measure: stream one token's 480 slices to the FPGA and time end-to-end tok/s.

Vector-quantize expert weights into 256-entry codebooks so each matmul becomes a table lookup, and pair two weights per entry (product VQ) so one gather+add serves two MACs, halving inner-loop ops: this cuts effective MACs to 6 GFLOP-equivalent and expert bytes to 0.65 GB/token, lifting the I/O-bound ceiling from ~1.2 to ~3.7 tok/s (compute would allow ~9), so I/O still binds but at 3x the old rate—verify the 1-2 perplexity cost by VQ-ing one layer's experts and benchmarking LUT-gather vs FP matmul on 4 cores.

Prefill I/O is the bottleneck: expert-major prefill reads ~69 GB once at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s. Move it off the critical path—during idle time, prefill the user's predicted next prompt and persist the KV cache (500-token prefix, 4-bit, ~1–2 GB). On request, reload at 2.4 GB/s in <1 s, cutting TTFT from 29 s to ~1 s. Decode bytes/token are unchanged, so throughput isn't 3x—only TTFT is, which is the objective. Cost: stale-cache misses on 5–21% cross-prompt hits; warm top-3 predicted prefixes.

Stripe each token's expert reads across local NVMe and a second LAN machine's RAM, but the real bound is compute (4.6 tok/s), so striping alone can't reach 3x. Fix: make the LAN machine a remote expert cache AND a compute peer—split the 48 layers 24/24 across both CPUs. Each side computes its half's 6 GFLOP/token, doubling aggregate compute to ~110 GFLOP/s → 9.2 tok/s ceiling. Expert bytes split too: each side reads only its 240 slices ≈0.65 GB at local 2.4 GB/s ≈0.27 s, overlapped with compute. Steady state ~7 tok/s aggregate, ~2.3x over 4 tok/s. But rank truncation plus low-bit residuals is a real approximation—fine-tuning recovers quantization, not basis error—so budget a perplexity rise, and if rank must grow, residual bytes grow and the 3x shrinks. Exit at layer 12, not 16: 4x fewer layers gives 0.33 GB/token (~7 tok/s) and 3 GFLOP/token (~18 tok/s), clearing 3x over 2 tok/s, while 16 only reaches ~5.5 tok/s. Memory fits 8 GB. Quality cost is real—keep full-depth fallback for low-confidence tokens. Cheapest first measurement: on 200 held-out prompts, log which layer's residual already matches final logits to find achievable exit depth before training.

Move expert matvec onto the storage: a SmartSSD-class FPGA-in-drive or CXL PIM card holds expert weights and applies gate/up/down in situ, returning only activation-sized results (~KBs), so the 1.3 GB/token of expert bytes never crosses PCIe. The bound attacked is I/O: today 480×2.7 MB=1.3 GB/token ÷2.4 GB/s≈0.54 s→1.9 tok/s; in situ, host reads ~0 expert bytes, and the 12 GFLOP/token expert GEMV runs on the card's FPGA at its own rate, not the laptop's. Two cards each sustaining ~6 GFLOP/token half → decode ~9 tok/s, ~4.7x. Bytes removed once, FLOPS added once.

Factor each layer's 10 active experts into one shared rank-64 basis B plus per-expert residual codes, cutting bytes ~4.3x (1.3GB→0.3GB) and active FLOPs ~3x. This shifts the binding bound to I/O at ~8 tok/s, ~2-4x over the 2-4 tok/s target. Cheapest validation: SVD one layer's 10 experts, check residual energy at r=64, and measure one-token end-to-end latency.

Batch all 480 expert-slice preads concurrently into a pinned buffer to exploit memory-level parallelism, but bandwidth alone caps you near 3.8 tok/s; the real win is cutting bytes/token. Pin the 1.9 GB dense weights plus a 12 GB LRU expert slab, issuing only ~4 non-resident slices per token as concurrent preads—dropping bytes/token from 1.3 GB to ~0.5 GB, reaching ~10 tok/s with no quality loss. First measure 480 concurrent vs serial preads to confirm achieved bandwidth.

Put the 69 GB expert store on ZNS NVMe as one 2.7 MB zone-aligned record per expert, read via io_uring O_DIRECT batched per layer, eliminating FTL read-modify-write and GC on the read path. This removes the mmap page-fault bottleneck (0.34 GB/s) and hits the measured 2.4 GB/s large-read rate: ~29 s for ~69 GB prefill versus ~100+ s TTFT now, a 3-4x cut attacking I/O, not compute. No weight quality cost; only install-time repacking. First measurement: 100 experts aligned, io_uring-read 480 slices for one layer, compare GB/s to mmap.

Factor each layer's 512 experts as W_e ≈ B·c_e, keeping one shared basis B per layer in RAM and only small per-expert coefficient codes on NVMe—cutting bytes per token rather than caching. With codes at 1/3 of each slice, a token reads 0.43 GB instead of 1.3 GB (0.18 s vs 0.54 s at 2.4 GB/s), lifting I/O to ~5.5 tok/s. Basis projection adds ~2 GFLOP/token, giving ~3.9 tok/s—pair with 40% expert pruning to reach ~4.6 tok/s and clear 3x. First: SVD one layer, sweep rank, record bytes and error, then time one token.

The LAN link, not local NVMe, becomes the new bottleneck: 10GbE (~1.1 GB/s) makes the 0.9 GB remote-RAM expert transfer ~0.8 s, too slow; even 25GbE/Thunderbolt (~2.5 GB/s) yields only ~1.7x, not 3x. Hitting 3x needs ≥40GbE, which the laptop lacks. Cheapest first measurement: stream one real prompt's 0.9 GB expert set laptop-to-laptop over the actual link and time sustained throughput plus remote cache hit rate.

VQ codes don't remove the bound: at 2.5-3 bits you get ~3.5x on I/O but compute (4.6 tok/s) binds, landing at ~3-4 tok/s. Attack the decode bound with a LUT kernel: keep experts at 4.3 bits but precompute per-layer 256-entry LUTs over 8-bit activations, so matvec becomes table gathers (no multiplies), moving compute ceiling to ~15-20 tok/s. Still I/O-bound, so also LUT-quantise activations to 8-bit and store experts at 2-bit codes: ~0.5 GB/token at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 0.21 s → ~4.5 tok/s, ~3.5x. Verify top-1 ≥95%; first measure one layer, 512 experts, 100 tokens.

For 500-token TTFT, prefill touches most experts, so attack prefill bytes: issue each layer's expert reads as many concurrent async preads (QD≥32) into a shared buffer, running expert-major so each expert streams once per layer for all routed tokens. At QD≥32 the drive's 5 GB/s ceiling is reachable, cutting 69 GB of expert bytes to ~14 s; batched compute then binds at ~19 s, giving TTFT ≈ 19 s vs ~44 s (~2.3x). To clear 3x, raise QD with 4 MiB-aligned expert blobs and run prefill at top-4 (6→2.4 TFLOP, ~8 s), yielding ~14 s (~3.1x)—but measure task accuracy, since top-4 prefill changes prompt

Caching alone can't reach 3x: the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling binds even at zero I/O. Cut FLOPs with top-4 experts (11.5 tok/s ceiling, I/O-bound ~4.5 tok/s), then overlap ARC-resident hot experts (~40% of slices) with reads to hit ~7.7 tok/s, ~2-3.8x. Recover quality with top-10 fallback on low router confidence; at f=0.2 that's ~3.5 tok/s, marginal over 4 tok/s. First measure: log expert IDs and router confidence on one 500-token prompt, replay ARC vs LRU at 22 GB, sweep the fallback threshold.

The overhead is the kernel's per-fault work, not read rate. Pad each expert's 3 tensors into one 1 MiB-aligned block and serve prefill via userfaultfd with a registered, pre-populated 1 MiB-aligned region, so each expert arrives as one 4 MiB-class read (2.4 GB/s) with zero per-slice fault/mmap bookkeeping. Prefill streams 69 GB once: 69/2.4=29 s vs 44 s, ~1.5x (compute 19 s, so max(29,19)=29 s). For 3x, add top-4 prefill routing: 28 GB→12 s, compute 8 s, TTFT≈12 s (~3.7x), at some quality cost on hard prompts and +11% disk. Cheapest test: time 1000 userfaultfd-served aligned 1 MiB expert reads

Put the 69 GB expert store in a CXL-attached DRAM pool so expert reads hit ~30 GB/s instead of 2.4 GB/s, cutting the 1.3 GB/token transfer from 0.54 s to ~0.04 s. But compute then binds at 4.6 tok/s, only ~1.2–2.3x over the 2–4 tok/s best path—so also cut compute: run prefill and decode at top-4 experts instead of 10 (4.8 GFLOP/token → 11.5 tok/s, 2.9–5.7x) for ~1–2 point quality loss on hard tokens. Cheapest first measurement: tmpfs-mount the experts on a 128 GB box and measure top-4 tok/s and prefill time before buying a CXL expander.

Keep the async-pipelined-read core, but fix the arithmetic and the bound. At 16 GB the binding limit is compute: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, so I/O overlap alone cannot reach 3x. Use the pipeline only to remove the serial stall, and cut FLOPs to raise the ceiling: run decode at top-4 of 10 experts (4.8 GFLOP/token → 11.5 tok/s ceiling). Bytes/token fall to ~0.52 GB; with 55% predicted prefetch overlapped under compute, synchronous misses are ~0.23 GB. Quality cost: top-4 routing loses accuracy; measure perplexity. First measurement: queue-depth sweep plus end-to-end tok/s at top-4

Prefill at top-k=4 cuts expert FLOPs 2.5x (6→2.4 TFLOP, 109→44 s). To clear 3x, pack the 4 experts' gate/up rows into one AVX-512 block so each load feeds 4 FMAs, plus prefetch the contiguous stream: ~1.3x throughput, giving 2.4 TFLOP÷(55×1.3)≈34 s, ~3.2x. FLOP cut and throughput multiply—no double-count. Risk: shallow routing may hurt hard prompts; decode unchanged. Test: time one layer at k=4 vs k=10, with/without lane-packing, 500-token prompt.

The 2-4 tok/s path is I/O-bound (1.3 GB/token at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 0.54 s vs. 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling), so the only route to ≥3x is cutting bytes/token ~3x, not overlapping. Within a sequence, k=8 consecutive tokens share 29/64 expert slices; a sequence-scoped ARC-style cache holds those 29 slices across the 8 tokens, reading each once per 8 tokens: 1.3 GB → 0.16 GB/token (~8x fewer bytes, ~0.07 s I/O). Compute then binds at 4.6 tok/s — still short of 3x — so also run top-4 instead of top-10 per layer during those groups: FLOPs fall 0.4x, lifting the ceiling to 11.5 tok/s, reaching ~8-10 tok/s. Qua

Low-rank factorise only the expert share of expert GEMMs: with d≈2048, r=64, U(Vx) costs ~0.5M vs ~8.4M FLOPs (~16x less), cutting total from 12 to ~4.5 GFLOP/token, prefill 109s→~41s, decode ~12 tok/s, and 4-bit factors ~16x smaller so 8GB stops binding. Risk: rank-64 on 4.3-bit experts may cost several perplexity points—validate per layer. Cheapest test: profile one layer's FLOP split, SVD its 10 hot experts, measure reconstruction error and real per-token FLOPs.

This targets the I/O bound, not compute: the 12 GFLOP/token wall (4.6 tok/s) can't be halved by 2-bit weights without 2-bit SIMD kernels. The honest win is the 8 GB I/O-bound regime, capped by expert bytes. Store each expert as a resident 2-bit base plus 2-bit enhancement, but keep bases only for a pinned subset: 24 GB ≈ 75% resident, 25% streamed. Per token, ~75% of 480 slices hit resident base (0 bytes); ~120 stream base+enhancement (~0.30 GB) plus enhancement for top-4 experts/layer (~0.24 GB) ≈ 0.54 GB/token vs 1.3 GB — 2.4x fewer bytes, ~5-9 tok/s, clearing 3x. Quality: ~0.5-1 pt drop. Fi

The real ceiling is 4.6 tok/s (~2.5x), not 3x: at 8 GB, 1.3 GB/token at 2.4 GB/s gives 1.85 tok/s I/O-bound; 2-bit residuals (2.5x) cut to ~0.52 GB/token → 0.22 s → 4.6 tok/s, now compute-bound at 12 GFLOP/55 GFLOP/s. Residual reconstruction is cheap (~0.5 GFLOP/token, negligible), so it doesn't lift that bound—claim 8 GB only. This is lossy residual requantization, not lossless (ruled out at 1.03x); the win must be measured. Cheapest first test: cluster one layer's 512 experts, quantize residuals to 2 bits, report reconstruction MSE and one-prompt perplexity delta before committing.

Apply the DB zone-map/index-only plan to the router: keep each layer's tiny gate matrix resident, run all 48 gates on the previous layer's predicted hidden to get candidate expert ids, then batch-pread only the union of survivors, skipping low-score experts before reading any weights (late materialisation). At precision 0.55, ~45% of predicted ids are wrong and skipped and 42% repeats collapse, cutting bytes/token from 1.3 GB to ~0.41 GB. Compute then binds at 4.6 tok/s; dropping to top-6 experts/layer reaches ~7.6 tok/s (~3x) at a cost of 2–4 pts on hard prompts. First measure predicted-vs-ac

Prefill TTFT is compute-bound: 6 TFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s. Add a mid-range FPGA (~1.2 TFLOP/s INT8) to reach ~1.25 TFLOP/s, cutting the bound to ~4.8 s; with expert streaming (69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s) overlapped, TTFT ≈ 29 s, still ~3.7x better. Cheapest check: time one 512×512×512 INT8 matmul on a $300 FPGA board vs the CPU's 55 GFLOP/s.

Factor each layer's 512 experts as shared basis B (rank r) plus per-expert residuals, but pick r from measured residual energy, not assertion. Stack experts, SVD, keep r where residual energy ≤10% (start r=64/512). Per token: B·x once per layer, then each of 10 routed experts applies only its rank-r residual. FLOPs/token ≈ 48×22·r·d; at d=4096, r=64 ≈ 0.28 GFLOP vs 12 — but only if residuals are truly low-rank; otherwise FLOPs stay ~12 and the 4.6 tok/s wall stands. The 3x is conditional on measured residual rank. Cheapest test: SVD one layer at r=64, measure residual energy on 100 real tokens

Run prefill expert-major: stream each expert once across all 500 prompt tokens with an int8 AVX2 dequant-dot kernel, attacking the prefill I/O bound that sets TTFT. Baseline 500×1.3 GB ≈ 650 GB at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 271 s; expert-major loads 69 GB once ≈ 29 s. Compute is 6 TFLOP at ~311 GFLOP/s ≈ 19 s, so I/O still binds and overlap is unnecessary: TTFT ≈ 29 s, ~9x. First measure one layer expert-major on 500 tokens, int8 vs 4.3-bit, and confirm batched GFLOP/s.

Prefill the 500 tokens in one expert-major pass: per layer, stream each of the 512 experts once (69 GB total) and apply it to every prompt position routed to it. That is 69 GB ÷ 1.56 GB/s ≈ 44 s of I/O, but it overlaps the 6 TFLOP compute (≈109 s at 55 GFLOP/s), so TTFT ≈ max(44,109) ≈ 109 s, not 44+109. Cache each layer's expert set and KV to disk as you go; the k=8 same-prefix union (29 of 64 slices) means later tokens and turns read only the delta, not 69 GB. Quality cost: none (exact, same weights). Cheapest test: log unique experts per layer over the 500-token prompt; if union ≪ 512×48, e

Stream the 69 GB expert set once, expert-major, sequentially through a Zoned Namespace so the FTL never amplifies: 69/2.4 = 29 s versus 650 GB scattered = 271 s. Then exploit routing locality: 8 consecutive tokens share only 29 of 64 expert slices, so run prefill in 8-token blocks, loading each routed expert once per block and applying it to all positions. Expert bytes drop ~2.2x (650→~295 GB, ~123 s) and expert FLOPs fall from 6 to ~2.7 TFLOP (~49 s). TTFT ≈ max(29 s I/O, 49 s compute) ≈ 49 s, a ~5.5x gain, exact for routed experts. First measure: time one layer's 8-token-block stream plus ma

PQ must exploit low-rank structure, not just 4-bit codes: 4.3→4 bits is only 1.07x, but a shared low-rank basis plus 4-bit PQ residuals gives ~2.5x fewer bytes. Even so, 3x decode is unreachable on 4 cores—compute binds after I/O shrinks. The defensible claim is ~2.4x TTFT: PQ cuts prefill's ~69 GB to ~28 GB, and expert-major streaming touches each expert once per layer, so TTFT ≈18 s vs ~44 s. Verify 4-bit residuals add ~0.1–0.2 perplexity; first measure PQ on one layer for bytes and output drift.

Session-scoped expert residency doesn't clear 3x: 29/64 union is per k=8 block, so per-token bytes are 1.3GB×(29/64)/8, but you can't also claim the 2.2x grouping — that's the already-found grouped-decode idea, and dividing by 29/64 then by 8 double-counts the same reuse. Compute binds at 4.6 tok/s anyway. Instead, attack the TTFT bound directly with prompt caching to disk borrowed from web session caches: cache the KV + the exact expert set touched by a 500-token prompt's prefill. First visit pays ~29s (69GB at 2.4GB/s); repeat/similar prompts skip prefill entirely, hitting TTFT ≈ decode of t

Delta-coding expert weights fails (1.03x, near-independent weights). The transferable codec move: use layer L's routing logits as a motion vector to speculatively prefetch layer L+1's experts (measured 0.55 precision), overlapping the 2.4 GB/s read with compute—hiding ~55% of the 0.54 s/token I/O, giving ~2x, not 3x. To reach 3x, also cut bytes via residual coding against the same expert id in the adjacent layer (layers correlate, unlike random experts); measure first—if residuals aren't ≥2x smaller, ship prefetch-only. Hedge: verify 0.55 precision on your own prompts.

Put experts on a second LAN machine and fetch per token over RDMA — the only lever that removes the local-disk ceiling rather than shaving it. Remote: 1.3 GB/token ÷ ~5 GB/s ≈ 0.26 s, ~3.8 tok/s, but compute floor (12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 0.22 s) caps it ~2.7 tok/s. To clear 3x, also route top-4 instead of top-10 (4.8 GFLOP → 0.09 s): max(0.26, 0.09) = 0.26 s → ~3.8 tok/s. Dense 1.9 GB stays local. First measure a single 1.3 GB RDMA read: if <0.3 s, build it.

Attack the 8 GB disk-bytes bound with asymmetric vector quantisation on expert weights: 8-weight blocks coded as one index into a 256-entry codebook, giving ~1.3 bits/weight and cutting expert bytes ~3.3x (1.3 GB/token → 0.39 GB), while dense 1.9 GB stays resident. This attacks the I/O bound, not the 55 GFLOP/s compute bound: prefill is compute-bound at ~109 s, so VQ cannot cut TTFT, only decode. Quality risk is real—expect several % perplexity without a short fine-tune, a prerequisite not free. First measurement: VQ one expert's three tensors, measure actual disk bytes and perplexity on 100 t

Build a resident per-layer zone map at install time: compact metadata per expert (id, gate-weight quantiles from calibration) in ~200 KB index. At decode, use the router's gate vector as a query predicate to decide which experts to materialize before any 2.7 MB read—late materialization. Skip experts below a threshold calibrated against measured output divergence, not gate magnitude alone. Dropping bottom-4-of-10 cuts bytes/token 1.3→0.78 GB (~0.5 s at 1.56 GB/s), ~2x tok/s, under the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling. Validate speed and quality in one pass: on 200 tokens, log gate weights and per-exp

Put the full 69 GB expert set in one LAN peer's RAM and stream each layer's ~10 experts over RDMA, pipelining layer l+1's fetch under layer l's compute. This attacks the 8 GB I/O wall: local 1.3 GB/token ÷ 2.4 GB/s = 0.54 s; remote 1.3 GB ÷ 5 GB/s = 0.26 s, overlapped with 0.22 s compute → 0.26 s/token ≈ 3.8 tok/s. That is only ~1.5x, so the peer must also supply compute: run the expert matmuls on the peer's CPU (it already holds the weights), returning only ~10×6 MB activations/layer. Peer compute 12 GFLOP/token at 55 GFLOP/s = 0.22 s, overlapped with 0.26 s fetch → 0.26 s/token, still 3.8 to

Treat experts as predictive-coded video: pin prior-token experts as keyframes, union-load across k=8 tokens (29/64 of naive bytes) — don't multiply by 0.58, since the 42% repeat is the same temporal correlation union-loading exploits. That gives ~0.59 GB/token ≈ 2.6 tok/s I/O, still under the 4.6 tok/s compute bound. To break compute, run the 10-of-512 router but execute only top-4 experts for decode, cutting FLOPs 40% (7.6 tok/s ceiling); with top-4 union (~0.24 GB) I/O drops to ~0.15 s ⇒ ~6.5 tok/s. Cost: top-4 decode loses ~1-2 benchmark points — measure it. Cheapest test: 200 tokens, log e

Decode is compute-bound at 4.6 tok/s (12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s), so I/O tricks can't reach 3x. Offload the MoE's expert GEMVs to a CXL-attached PIM accelerator that does the multiply-accumulate where the weights sit, so the 55 GFLOP/s host ceiling stops binding; keep the dense 1.9 GB on the CPU, stream each token's 1.3 GB expert set once into the PIM pool (~64 GB/s), and effective decode compute rises to ~200 GFLOP/s → ~16 tok/s, ~3.5x, at no quality cost. First measurement: one layer's 10-expert GEMV on a PIM/CXL dev board vs CPU.

Keep a resident low-rank basis per expert and stream only the residual delta, using per-block zone maps (min/max/energy) to skip residual blocks below tolerance—attacking the I/O bound. Per token: 480 slices × 2.7 MB = 1.3 GB at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 0.54 s (~1.9 tok/s); skipping 70% of residual blocks with a ~30%-of-bytes basis gives ~0.39 GB → 0.16 s → ~6 tok/s (~3x). Gate first: on one layer, measure rank-8 residual energy and zone-map skip rate—if residual >30% or skip <50%, the 3x fails.

Prefill's single 69 GB pass can populate a pinned 21.5 GB expert working set (31% of experts), cutting decode I/O from 1.3 to ~0.9 GB/token (~2.7 tok/s), but that's only ~2.5x—not 3x. The 3x requires also capturing the 42% previous-token repeat and 55% layer-prediction hits in the resident set, dropping effective misses to ~0.5 GB/token so compute binds at 4.6 tok/s (~3x over 1.5 tok/s baseline). Cheapest test: on one 500-token prompt, log prefill's unique-expert union, decode overlap, and resident hit rate—if hit rate <60%, the 3x fails.

Product-quantize expert weights to ~1.1 bits/weight so all 69 GB → ~18 GB and fits RAM; prefill then reads zero disk, killing the 29–44 s I/O floor. But compute still binds: 500×12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s, so also run prefill at top-4 experts (6→2.4 TFLOP ≈ 44 s), giving >3x TTFT. Quality cost: lossy at 1.1 bits, expect perplexity rise. Cheapest test: PQ one layer's 512 experts, measure reconstruction error and one-prompt perplexity delta. Outside your control: PQ quality loss may exceed tolerance; hedge by mixing 2-bit for sensitive layers.

Split experts by id: the laptop keeps a hot set resident; a LAN peer holds the rest in RAM and computes those expert FFNs, returning only KB activations over RDMA/TCP—so the wire carries results, not 0.9MB weights. The peer's RAM is the key: it must hold its ~half of experts resident (a 64GB peer holds ~34GB, half of 69GB), so its reads are RAM-speed, not NVMe. Then per-token wall time = max(local I/O 0.65GB/2.4GB/s≈0.27s, peer compute 6GFLOP/55GFLOP/s≈0.11s, LAN) ≈0.27s → ~3.7 tok/s. That's only ~2x, so also cut local bytes: keep the 42%-repeat experts pinned locally (LRU hit), dropping local

Overlap the next layer's 10 expert preads (3×0.9MB) as one deep async batch into a pinned, 4KiB-aligned double buffer while the current GEMM runs, keeping NVMe queue depth high so the CPU never stalls on a single 1MB read. This hides the 4.5ms GEMM behind the 11ms load, leaving ~6.5ms/layer → ~3.2 tok/s (~1.7x). Add the 0.55 predictor (prefetch predicted experts, 42% repeats hit LRU) to cut issued bytes ~45% → ~2.9 tok/s. Measure one layer: 10 preads at queue depth 10 vs 1, timed against its GEMM.

The 55 GFLOP/s ceiling is measured, not FP32-specific, so don't assume VNNI multiplies it—cut FLOPs instead: run expert GEMMs at int8 with AVX-512 VNNI (vpdpbusd) and measure actual sustained GOPS on this CPU. If VNNI sustains even 110 GOPS, 12 GFLOP/token gives 9 tok/s, 3x over 2-4. Cheapest first step: time one layer's expert GEMM int8-VNNI vs FP32 on the laptop to confirm the real multiplier. This removes the compute bound only where RAM holds the weights.

Put the 69 GB of expert weights in a CXL 2.0 DRAM expander so the CPU streams experts at DRAM bandwidth instead of NVMe. This attacks the prefill I/O bound: 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s TTFT floor becomes 69 ÷ 12 GB/s ≈ 5.8 s (using a conservative 12 GB/s effective CXL.mem rate, not the optimistic 25). Decode: 1.3 GB/token at 12 GB/s ≈ 0.11 s, so compute (4.6 tok/s) binds instead of I/O. Quality cost: none — bit-identical weights, same routing. Cheapest first measurement: borrow one CXL expander, run the 500-token prefill, and time 0.9 MB expert-slice reads (not bulk sequential) against the 2.4 GB/

Decode is I/O-bound, not compute-bound: 1.3 GB/token ÷ 2.4 GB/s = 0.54 s read vs 0.22 s compute (~1.8 tok/s). Use a codec-style delta scheme: previous layer's experts predict next layer's at 0.55 precision, so prefetch the predicted 0.72 GB during the 0.22 s compute window, then read only ~0.58 GB of misses → 0.24 s, ~4.1 tok/s (2.3x). Lossless: wrong predictions are discarded. First measure per-layer predicted-vs-actual expert overlap on one prompt to confirm 0.55 locally.

Decode is compute-capped (12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 4.6 tok/s), so I/O tuning alone can't pass it. Use a trained per-token, per-layer early-exit gate to run only 2 of 10 experts on confident layers: bytes ~0.26 GB → ~9 tok/s, compute 2.4 GFLOP → ~23 tok/s; ceiling min≈9 tok/s, ~3x. Validate on 200 held-out tokens: log gate confidence vs top-10 agreement and tok/s at 8 GB.

Keep the covering-copy idea, but make the 2-bit copy replace the 4.3-bit read, not add to it. Store a 2-bit shadow of all 69 GB of experts (~32 GB) on NVMe and never read the base during decode. A 2-bit slice is ~0.21 MB, so 480 slices/token ≈ 0.1 GB/token; at 2.4 GB/s that is ~0.04 s ≈ 24 tok/s of I/O. Compute now binds: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, so cut to top-4 experts (≈4.8 GFLOP/token) → ~11 tok/s, ~3x over 2–4 tok/s. Quality: 2-bit costs ~1–2 perplexity points; recover by re-reading the 4.3-bit top-2 slices only (~0.9 MB, negligible). First measurement: quantise 4 layers, m

Prefill I/O sets TTFT: 500 tokens touch ~all 69GB once, ~29s at 2.4GB/s. Stream experts through a NUMA-pinned huge-page ring buffer sized to L3 with non-temporal SIMD loads, repacked contiguously at install, and issue one deep io_uring queue (depth 64) of sequential 0.9MB reads; the prefetcher plus MLP hits the drive's large-read ceiling (~5GB/s → 14s, ~2x). Combine with the measured 42% same-token expert repeat by caching the previous token's 480 slices in the ring: prefill reads ~0.58×69 ≈ 40GB → ~8s, ~3.6x over 29s, bit-exact. Cheapest test: time a 69GB sequential-aligned sweep at queue dep

TTFT is set by prefill compute, not decode I/O: 500×12 GFLOP = 6 TFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s. Run the matmul in int8/fp8 instead of FP32—the 55 GFLOP/s ceiling is an FP32 number, and int8/fp8 tensor throughput on the same 4 cores is ~3–4x higher. Keep 4.3-bit weights for storage, dequantize tiles on the fly. That lifts the ceiling to ~180 GFLOP/s: 6 TFLOP ÷ 180 ≈ 33 s, a ~3.3x TTFT cut, with I/O unchanged (69 GB at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s, now co-binding). Quality cost is only int8/fp8 rounding (<0.5 benchmark points); verify per-layer. First test: time one layer's prefill matmul FP32 vs int8, confirm

Prefill compute, not I/O, sets TTFT: 6 TFLOP÷55 GFLOP/s≈109 s vs 69 GB÷2.4 GB/s≈29 s. An FPGA expert-GEMV engine MACing each 0.9 MB slice in on-card DRAM, fed by PCIe 3.0 x8 (~6 GB/s), sustains ~200 GFLOP/s only because each slice does ~30 MFLOP (~8 FLOP/byte). That drops compute to ~30 s, matching I/O's 29 s: TTFT≈30 s, a 3.6x cut. Don't also stripe NVMes—that double-counts. First measure: stream one layer's 10 slices over PCIe into the FPGA, timing end-to-end GEMV vs CPU.

Prefill compute, not I/O, is the TTFT floor: 6 TFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s vs 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s. Session-aware idle-time background prefill can help, but the 3x gain must be hit-rate-weighted: expected TTFT = (1−h)·109 s + h·~2 s, so 3x (≤36 s) needs h ≥ 0.68. Cross-prompt hot-list hits are only 5–21%, so key on exact/shared prefixes within a session, where reuse is high.

Keep the ARC ghost-list cache but make it per-sequence-window, sized to 24 GB (1.9 GB dense + ~20 GB experts); ghost-hit feedback learns reuse distance online since offline hot lists transfer only 5-21%. Bytes/token: 278 compulsory slices + ~125 prefetchable (0.55 cross-layer precision) + admitted-window misses (29/64 of 278) + prefetch error ≈ 0.39 GB/token → 6.1 tok/s I/O at 2.4 GB/s, but compute caps at 4.6 tok/s, so the real ceiling is compute (~1.5-2.3x, not 3x). To clear 3x, admit only 6-of-10 experts per layer: 0.6× compute → 7.7 tok/s ceiling, window cache keeps bytes ≈0.24 GB/token →

Serve experts from a LAN peer's RAM over Ethernet, not local NVMe—but cut compute per token too. Stream only the 10 routed experts per layer (unchanged), yet run top-k=4 during decode: 12→~4.8 GFLOP/token, allowing ~11 tok/s. I/O: 4 experts/layer × 48 × 0.9 MB ≈ 0.52 GB/token ÷ 5 GB/s ≈ 0.10 s → ~9.5 tok/s. Both bounds clear 3x over 2–4 tok/s. Peer needs 69 GB RAM—use a 128 GB desktop, not a 16 GB laptop. Quality cost: top-k 10→4 loses accuracy; measure on your eval. Cheapest first test: one peer serving one layer's 4 experts over TCP, time 192 slice fetches, confirm ≥5 GB/s end-to-end.

Prefill compute sets TTFT: 6 TFLOP÷55 GFLOP/s≈109s vs 69GB÷2.4GB/s≈29s. Double-buffer next-layer expert preads under the current-layer GEMM so the 29s I/O hides inside compute (138s→109s). That's only 1.3x; the 3x must come from cutting FLOPs, not stacking an unproven SIMD speedup. 55 GFLOP/s is the practical SIMD ceiling, so exploit the 4-core cache hierarchy: run each expert's GEMM on 4 KiB-aligned, L2-resident tiles so the active 1.3GB streams through L2/L3 without re-fetch, plus hardware prefetch on the double-buffered preads. Honest arithmetic: 109s compute floor, I/O hidden, TTFT≈109s vs

Put the 69 GB of experts on computational-storage (CSD) drives that run each routed expert's GEMV in-flash, so host ships only ~10 activation vectors per layer and receives ~KB back—expert bytes never cross PCIe. This attacks the I/O bound, not compute: host traffic drops from ~432 MB/token to ~2.4 MB (~180x less), leaving decode limited by in-flash GEMV latency. Same weights, zero approximation. First measurement: on one CSD dev board, time a single 0.9 MB expert GEMV in-flash; if <0.5 ms, 480 slices ≈ 0.24 s/token (>3x over 2–4 tok/s). Risk: flash-controller GEMV throughput is vendor-fixed—b

3x needs cutting expert count, not bytes: zone-map each expert's gate-norm range (~2KB/layer) and skip experts that can't beat the current top-10 score—index-only pruning over 512 floats in L2. Pruning 30% of 10 experts gives ~0.91 GB/token and ~8.4 GFLOP/token, raising compute ceiling to ~6.5 tok/s (1.6–3.2x), attacking both bounds. Cost: approximate top-k, small perplexity hit—measure it. First test: 200 tokens, check how many true top-10 fall outside the pruned set; hedge with an 8-expert floor and per-domain zone maps.

Compute all 512 gate logits first (dense, resident), then read only top-4 experts: 480→192 slices, 1.3→0.52 GB/token → 0.83→0.33 s at 1.56 GB/s (2.5x I/O); FLOPs 12→4.8 GFLOP → compute ceiling 4.6→11.5 tok/s. On the 2-4 tok/s path this lands ~3-4x. Cost: top-4 vs top-10 loses a few quality points; recover by rescaling gate logits. Test: log gate logits on 200 tokens, measure top-4 recall of top-10 output and tok/s. Risk: real routers may not concentrate mass in top-4 — hedge by falling back to top-10 when top-4 gate mass < threshold.

Put the full 69 GB expert set in a second LAN machine's RAM and ship only hidden activations (~12 KB/layer), so the network carries activations, not weights. Prerequisite: a 64 GB+ RAM box (e.g. 128 GB workstation); without it, the mechanism is unavailable. Arithmetic: remote streams 1.3 GB/token from RAM at ~40 GB/s ≈ 33 ms; compute 12 GFLOP/token at 200 GFLOP/s ≈ 60 ms; LAN 0.6 MB/token at 5 GB/s ≈ 0.1 ms, but 48 sequential RTTs at 0.5 ms = 24 ms unless pipelined—pipeline layers so RTT overlaps compute. Total ≈ 60–90 ms/token ≈ 11–16 tok/s, ≥3x over 2–4 tok/s. Quality cost: none for exact ma

Column-block each expert's gate/up/down matrices with per-block max-activation zone maps; at decode, read only blocks whose max exceeds a threshold, skipping dead intermediate dims—and since skipping dim d also skips row d of the down matrix, bytes and FLOPs fall together. With 50% dead blocks plus 42% cross-token block reuse, I/O drops to ~0.38 GB/token (~6.3 tok/s, 2.6x); reaching 60% dead clears 3x. First measurement: log per-layer, per-block activation magnitudes over 100 tokens; if byte-weighted dead fraction is under 55%, abandon.

Remote-memory RDMA plus pipelining hides wire latency behind compute, but the 4.6 tok/s compute cap blocks 3x alone; caching the 42% repeated experts cuts wire to ~0.75 GB and pairs with top-k 10→7 to reach ~6 tok/s—a real 3x over 2 tok/s, at a modest perplexity cost.

At 32 GB the wall is compute: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, and no byte trick moves it. The only real fix is offline: add a learned per-layer skip gate via mixture-of-depths, distilled from the full 125B, so ~half of 48 layers run per token—halving compute to ~6 GFLOP/token (9.2 tok/s ceiling) and bytes to 0.65 GB/token, giving ~3.7 tok/s on 8 GB, about 3x the I/O-bound baseline.

Cut active parameters per token instead of tuning eviction: an online learned cache over router confidence (ARC-style adaptive admission, not fixed top-k) sets per-layer k≈4, dropping compute to 4.8 GFLOP/token and raising the compute ceiling from 4.6 to ~11.5 tok/s. At 8 GB RAM the binding limit becomes I/O at ~4.6 tok/s; at 32 GB, compute at ~11.5 — both above the 2-4 tok/s baseline, but only ~1.2-2.3x, not 3x. The 3x target is unreachable within this mechanism; the gain is real but bounded. Quality cost: measurable perplexity rise; validate before shipping.

The 8 GB box is I/O-bound (~0.9 tok/s), not compute-bound (4.6 tok/s), so cut expert bytes structurally: upcycle the MoE into a dense ~6B specialist, same 12 GFLOP/token but zero 1.3 GB expert reads; at 4.3 bits the 6B is ~3.2 GB, resident in 8 GB with ~1 GB KV/activations/OS, hitting 55÷12 = 4.6 tok/s. That's only 2.3x over 2 tok/s, so also depth-distill 48→24 layers: 6 GFLOP/token → 9.2 tok/s, 4.6x. Quality drops on hard prompts; keep the MoE as fallback. First: convert 8 layers, confirm 3.2 GB stays resident, measure tok/s.

Your core move is right: on Gen4 the 69 GB read (~14 s) hides under prefill compute (~109 s), so pipelining expert loads across layers is free and the real lever is cutting prefill FLOPs. Close the 3x gap with a microarchitectural trick, not extra reuse: use AVX-512 VNNI/AMX-style int8 SIMD on the expert matmuls. Expert FLOPs are ~90% of 12 GFLOP/token; int8 SIMD gives ~4x throughput on those, so per-token cost ≈ 0.9×12/4 + 0.1×12 = 3.9 GFLOP-equivalent. 500 tokens × 3.9 = 1.95 TFLOP at 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 35 s, ~3.1x. Bytes still hide (14 s < 35 s). Quality cost: int8 expert weights, small perplexit

Persist full post-prefill state (KV + router/expert trace) as a session-aware precompute that pays off on the FIRST token: during idle time, speculatively prefill likely session prompts (user history/editor buffer) to disk; on arrival, match shared prefix, reload, decode from matched position. This attacks the 29s prefill I/O floor: reload 1.5GB at 2.4GB/s (~0.6s) + one decode step (~0.7s) ≈1.3s TTFT vs 29s (>20x); even 50% match gives ~15s (>3x). Lossless for matched prefixes; cost is wasted idle prefill on misses. First measure real session prompt-prefix overlap to estimate hit rate, then ti

Unpacking 4.3-bit slices on the same 4 cores is an uncounted tax that caps decode at 2-4 tok/s. Fix: pre-unpack experts to int8 at install (offline), so the hot loop is a plain int8 MAC at the true 55 GFLOP/s ceiling = 4.6 tok/s; bytes/token rises 1.3→2.4 GB but stays resident in 32 GB, so compute binds. Then reuse the prior token's slices as a delta reference (42% repeat exactly) to cut effective compute to ~7 GFLOP/token → ~7.8 tok/s, 2-4x. Quality: int8 per-channel, <0.1 ppl. First measure one layer's 10 slices: unpacked vs int8-resident vs delta-reused.

Repack each expert's 3×0.9 MB tensors into one 4 MiB-aligned blob and read it O_DIRECT via io_uring, bypassing the page cache. This attacks the TTFT bound, not decode: prefill reads ~69 GB, and O_DIRECT stops the page cache from evicting the dense weights and LRU, so the 8 GB stays available. Arithmetic: 69 GB at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s I/O floor; compute floor is 500×12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s, so I/O is not the binding term once reads are clean — TTFT is compute-bound at ~109 s, and the win is removing page-cache thrash that made prefill 4–7× slower than the 29 s floor. Quality cost: none, lossle

Pin the session's touched expert union in the 22 GB free after the 1.9 GB dense weights (~27 slices/layer), evicting cold slices, so decode reads ~0 instead of 540 ms and hits the 218 ms compute floor (4.6 tok/s). That alone is only ~1.5-2x, so pair it with the GFLOP cut the floor demands: decode at top-4 experts (12→~5 GFLOP/token), giving 55/5 ≈ 11 tok/s, ~3-5x over 2-4 tok/s. First measurement: log per-layer expert IDs over a 10-turn session, compute union vs 27-slice budget and hit rate.

Keep userfaultfd+io_uring fault-path, but target TTFT for 500-token prefill: I/O-bound at 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s. Lay experts as one 4 MiB-aligned blob per layer; during prefill map them via userfaultfd serviced by io_uring O_DIRECT registered-buffer reads at 2.4 GB/s instead of the 0.34 GB/s fault path—7x on the path gating prefill, not decode. 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s vs ÷ 0.34 ≈ 203 s, ~7x TTFT cut, clearing 3x with no reuse tricks. Quality cost: none—layout only, same weights, same routing. First measurement: one layer's 4 MiB blob, 1000 faults io_uring vs mmap, confirm ≥2 GB/s.

Move the active-expert matmul onto the drive (CSD/FPGA) so expert bytes never cross the bus—only MB activations return. This attacks the compute bound, not just I/O: prefill TTFT drops to ~18s (CPU-bound) vs 109s compute/29s I/O floor, ~3.5x; decode binds on CPU at 4.6 tok/s, still >3x the 2–4 tok/s path. First measurement: one FPGA on USB4 running a single 0.9 MB expert slice matmul—confirm ≥0.1 TFLOP/s and ≥1.5 GB/s internal read to validate the mechanism.

Scalable coding works only if the base isn't resident (34.5 GB > 32 GB): keep ~1.9 GB dense weights plus an LRU of reconstructed experts in RAM, with base+residual striped on NVMe—removing the 8 GB I/O bound but not the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling, so the honest claim is ~2x, compute-bound thereafter.

Use the router as a zone map over a column-store layout: store each expert's three tensors as separate columns and fetch only those whose router-weighted contribution exceeds a threshold, late-materialising the rest. This attacks I/O, not compute: skipping the two smaller tensors on 60% of slices cuts bytes/token from 1.3 GB to ~0.78 GB (1.7x), lifting I/O-bound decode from ~2-4 to ~3.5-7 tok/s, at ~1-2% perplexity cost. First measure: on one layer, log per-column router mass and verify a threshold skips ≥50% of columns while retaining ≥95% of mass.

At 32 GB, compute binds at 4.6 tok/s. Borrow motion compensation: predict layer L+1's expert output from layer L's activation, compute only residuals above threshold. Expert matmuls (~10 of 12 GFLOP/token) are skippable; skipping 75% gives ~11 tok/s (2.4x). Cheapest test: one layer, regress expert output on prior activation, report residual sparsity at fixed error—need ≥75% skip at <1% perplexity, else abandon.

Prefetch caps at ~1.8x; the real lever is userfaultfd: DAX-map the expert file from zoned-NVMe, io_uring-prefetch predicted next-layer experts (0.55 hit), and fault only the 45% mispredicted slices synchronously. Per token: 0.72 GB blocking ÷ 2.4 GB/s = 0.30 s, 0.58 GB hidden under 0.22 s compute → ~3.3 tok/s, no accuracy loss. Decode-only; TTFT stays 109 s. First measure: log io_uring vs compute timestamps over 200 tokens; if blocking fraction >0.45, 3x fails.

Treat the drive as a compute node, but not for matmul: CSD/PIM (~1–2 TOPS) can't run 12 GFLOP/token. Instead offload expert selection and partial-sum accumulation—the drive holds all 69 GB and, per layer, computes only the k-dim gate/up projections for the 10 routed experts, returning ~10 small vectors instead of 1.3 GB. Host does down-projection. This kills the 1.3 GB/token host read and 69 GB prefill read. Batch prefill on drive MACs too (~6 s TTFT vs 29 s), and group k=8 same-sequence partial sums to cut host compute 8x (~37 tok/s decode). Exact weights, only reordered accumulation. Cheapes

Gate scores are cheap (~4 MB), but top-10 needs all 512 scores, so zone maps can't skip down_proj without knowing the ranking. Late materialisation (rank all 512, then read only top-10) is already what routing does and avoids wasted reads on mispredicted experts—but it doesn't cut the true top-10's 1.3 GB, so no 3x. The compute ceiling (12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s) binds once I/O is fixed; no DB-lens trick removes it. Cheapest test: time gate-only vs full expert read on 100 tokens.

Apply double-buffering to the real bottleneck: prefill TTFT. While the user types, run only the prompt prefix through the router and pread predicted expert slices into the LRU cache, ordered by 0.55 next-layer precision. This is usage-pattern speculation, not I/O tuning. Prefill reads 69 GB at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s; idle warm-up moves ~55% off the critical path, leaving ~13 s I/O, now under the 109 s compute floor, so TTFT ≈ 109 s vs 138 s serial. Quality cost: none (exact weights; mispredictions just evict). Cheapest test: log predicted vs actual expert hits and pread bytes during a simulated 30 s

Keep int8/VNNI but make it real: TTFT = max(I/O, compute). I/O: 69→35 GB at 2.4 GB/s = 15 s. Compute: 6 TFLOP at 220 GFLOP/s = 27 s, so TTFT ≈ 27 s vs 109 s — 4x, compute-bound. But 220 GFLOP/s int8 needs ~220 GB/s weight feed; 4-core laptop DRAM gives ~50 GB/s → real ceiling ~50 GFLOP/s → ~120 s, no win. Streaming experts from NVMe (2.4 GB/s) fused dequant+matmul gives ~19 GFLOP/s, still short. Honest verdict: verify VNNI first — run a 4-core int8 GEMM microbenchmark and `lscpu | grep vnni`; if absent or <100 GFLOP/s, abandon. Quality: per-channel scales, router/dense fp16; expect ~1 perplexi

Put expert matmuls in computational-storage FPGAs on two U.2 NVMes (~34 GB of experts each) so weights never cross PCIe—only ~4 KB activations and partial sums. This removes the 8 GB-RAM I/O bound: 1.3 GB/token ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 0.54 s (~1.8 tok/s) collapses to compute-only 12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 0.22 s → 4.6 tok/s, a 2.5–3x gain. Cost: on-drive int8/int4 matmul vs 4.3-bit weights, ~0.5–1 pt perplexity; routing unchanged. First test: one FPGA drive, one layer's 512 experts, time a 10-expert int4 GEMV at batch 1—if it beats 55 GFLOP/s the bound is gone. Hedge: prototype on one drive before buying t

Make the LAN peer an expert compute server, not a byte store: split experts 256/256 per layer; each node runs its routed experts' matmuls and returns ~20KB activations. Traffic/token: 48×10×20KB ≈ 10MB over 10GbE ≈ 9ms, vs 1.3GB. Each node streams only its ~35GB half at 2.4GB/s → 0.65GB/token → ~0.27s; two 4-core nodes give 110 GFLOP/s → 9.2 tok/s ceiling. Net ~3.5–4 tok/s, >3x. Quality cost: none (exact math, just split). First measurement: time one layer's remote-expert RPC round-trip over the LAN. Outside your control: LAN latency/jitter and peer uptime—hedge by keeping the dense weights an

Keep all 69 GB of experts RAM-resident on peers; the laptop holds only 1.9 GB dense weights and ships activations. But one peer doing all expert matmuls caps at 4.6 tok/s (12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s), merely tying the compute ceiling. Split 48 layers across three peers (16 each, ~23 GB experts, 4 GFLOP/token) for 13.8 tok/s — 3.4x over 4 tok/s, with no quality loss beyond negligible fp accumulation-order differences. First measurement: time one peer serving 24 layers for one token over the real LAN; under 110 ms clears 3x.

Put the sparse-expert GEMV on a PCIe FPGA between NVMe and CPU: it streams the 480 expert slices, multiplies in place, and returns only ~10 KB/layer instead of 1.3 GB. The FPGA does the 12 GFLOP/token, so the 55 GFLOP/s CPU ceiling no longer applies; the I/O bound is unchanged (1.3 GB at 2.4 GB/s = 0.54 s → 1.8 tok/s), so require the FPGA to sustain 2.4 GB/s on 0.9 MB slices. That alone is not 3x, so also have the FPGA hold a 20 GB hot-expert cache in its DRAM: at 42% same-prompt reuse, ~0.75 GB/token → ~0.31 s → ~3.2 tok/s, ~3x over 2-4 tok/s, without stacking any forbidden union factor. Qual

Compute-bound at 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s; I/O tuning can't pass it. Cut FLOPs/token and raise effective FLOP/s via AVX-512 VNNI int8 expert matmuls—but measure, don't assume 4x; realistic gain on these small, latency-bound GEMMs is ~1.5–2x (~83–110 GFLOP/s). Pruning to 6-of-10 experts halves FLOPs to 7.2 GFLOP/token, giving ~11.5 tok/s compute ceiling; bytes (~0.78 GB/token at 5 GB/s ≈ 6 tok/s) land both near 6–11 tok/s, ≥3x over 2. TTFT stays compute-bound: prefill 500 tokens ≈ 6 TFLOP → ~110 s int8, ~65 s pruned. Cost: ~0.5–1 perplexity point; verify.

Treat the previous token's expert set as a reference frame and read only the residual, but make it a real codec with motion compensation: the previous layer's experts predict the next layer's at 0.55 precision, so prefetch the predicted set and read only misses. With 42% same-sequence repeat, resident plus predicted hits cover most of the 480 slices, cutting I/O toward ~0.4 GB/token (~0.15 s/token, ~6.5 tok/s), above the 4.6 compute ceiling—so compute now binds and the I/O bound is removed at zero quality cost, exact bytes. Cheapest test: log per-layer predicted-vs-actual expert overlap and ti

Int8 SIMD expert GEMMs remove the compute bound (~2x, ~620 GFLOP/s, prefill ~10s) but cannot beat the I/O floor: 69 GB at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29s, so TTFT stays ~29s and int8 alone fails. It only helps once bytes drop; cheapest check is timing one layer's int8 vs FP32 GEMM to confirm compute is no longer the limiter.

Prefill FLOPs are fixed, but speculative background warm-up during typing moves them off the critical path: run the model on the growing prompt prefix (cached to disk) while the user types, so at submit only the residual tail remains. TTFT drops from ~138s to ~5-14s (>3-10x), attacking the compute bound, not I/O. Quality cost: none (same weights, same tokens); only wasted work if the prompt is abandoned. Cheapest test: log keystroke-to-submit idle time and measure TTFT with vs without background prefill.

Compute, not I/O, is the ceiling: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, so no I/O fix clears 3x. Train a per-layer router (distilled from base layer outputs) running each token through ~16 of 48 layers, keeping all 10 experts: 4 GFLOP/token → ~13.7 tok/s, ~3.3x. Cheapest first measurement: on 50 held-out prompts, log router confidence and compare perplexity at 16 vs 48 layers before any retraining.

Cut compute, not I/O: low-rank expert factors (rank-64) slash FLOPs 32x, but streaming 0.45 GB/token at 2.4 GB/s caps you at ~5 tok/s — still >3x, so I/O binds, not compute. Cheapest test: factor layer 0's 10 experts, 50 prompts, go if ppl ≤ +1 and tok/s ≥ 3x.

Cut active parameters per token by model-structure surgery: route 6-of-10 experts and fold each layer's survivors into one shared rank-32 basis plus per-expert residuals. This attacks the compute bound, the binding one once I/O is fixed: 12 GFLOP/token × (6/10) × (32/64) ≈ 3.6 GFLOP/token, raising the cap from 4.6 to ~15 tok/s, with bytes falling to ~0.4 GB/token so decode lands near 8-12 tok/s, ~3x over the 2-4 tok/s path. Quality cost is real (2-4 benchmark points), recoverable with a short finetune; cheapest first measurement is perplexity on 1k tokens before writing any loader.

Compute, not I/O, binds at 32 GB: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, and bit-plane truncation can't help since FLOPs stay fixed. Instead, store a rank-8 sketch per expert (1/8 the FLOPs) and run the full slice only when the sketch residual exceeds a threshold—coarse-then-refine, like a delta frame. FLOPs/token = 1.5 + 10.5r; hitting 3x (≤4 GFLOP/token) needs r ≤ 0.24, so the threshold must gate out ≥76% of experts. Budget r≈0.2, not 0.4 (which yields only ~9.6 tok/s), since sketch error compounds superlinearly over 48 layers. First measurement: log sketch residual vs. full-output error o

Idle-time speculative prefill: while idle, continuously prefill the live session's own prompt prefix as the user types, persisting KV+expert set keyed by rolling prefix hash. On request, only the uncached tail is prefilled, so a 500-token already-typed prompt has tail≈0 and TTFT≈1s vs 44–109s (>40x), attacking the prefill I/O+compute bound. Works for arbitrary prompts because it warms the actual prefix, not guessed ones; exact KV, same weights, no quality loss. Cheapest measurement: time incremental prefix prefill + KV dump/reload.

Prefill compute sets TTFT: 500×12 GFLOP = 6 TFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s, vs 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s. Layout/quant tricks cut bytes, not FLOPs, so 3x (36 s) is unreachable that way. From the numerics lens, apply 2:4 structured sparsity plus 4-bit weights to expert FFNs: halves MACs, effective ~110 GFLOP/s → ~55 s (~2x), quality cost ~1–2 points. To actually clear 3x you must add FLOPs: a small GPU running the sparse expert kernels gets you past 36 s. Cheapest first measurement: time one 500-token prefill with 2:4-sparse 4-bit expert kernels on this laptop. Outside your control: whether the spars

Group tokens by expert before the matmul so one loaded expert slice serves k=8 tokens: bytes/token 10.4→4.7 GB (2.2x), I/O ~2.0 s/token, while compute stays 12 GFLOP/token (4.6 tok/s ceiling), so I/O and compute cross near 2 tok/s. Apply the same grouping to the dense path to amortize its 1.9 GB shared weights ~k-fold, cutting dense FLOPs ~2.5x and landing ~4.5-5 tok/s. Grouping is exact, no quality loss. First measure: one layer, k=8 vs k=1, union load and FLOPs on real hardware to see which binds.

Borrow late materialisation: keep a tiny per-expert sketch (~3 MB resident) as an index-only plan, score all 512 experts, and materialise only the top ~10 payloads as one coalesced block. This attacks I/O, not compute—but sketches only skip non-winners, so bytes/token fall only by the fraction of true experts ranked in top-10. At 0.55 precision you still read ~1.3 GB. To hit 3x you must cut payload bytes (3-bit slices: 1.3→0.9 GB) and combine with k=8 same-sequence union (29/64): ~0.05 GB/token, compute-bound at 4.6 tok/s. Cheapest first measurement: sketch top-10 recall vs true next-layer exp

Distill the MoE into one dense ~6B student and run it resident on the 12 GB GPU: this removes the I/O bound entirely (1.3 GB/token → 0) and moves decode to GPU compute, not the 55 GFLOP/s CPU ceiling. Arithmetic: 6B at 4.3 bits ≈ 3.2 GB, fits 12 GB VRAM alongside KV. CPU-only caps at 12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s; on GPU at ~5–10x the laptop's FLOPs: 4.6 × 5–10 ≈ 23–46 tok/s, i.e. 6–12x over the 2–4 tok/s best path. No factor double-counted. Quality cost: a few benchmark points; mitigate with on-policy distillation and route hard prompts back to the MoE.

Pin this prompt's top ~5 experts/layer (~0.65 GB) and reuse them twice: cut prefill's 69 GB read by the pinned fraction (~31%, 29s→~20s) and run their matmuls batched across all 500 positions, plus decode drops 1.3→0.65 GB/token (~3.7 tok/s). Honest: only ~1.5-2x decode, 4.6 tok/s ceiling untouched, no quality cost. First check: log per-layer expert IDs over one 500-token prompt; abandon if self-reuse <60%.

Your 3x claim double-counts: the k=8 union already assumes full slices, so stacking residual coding on top lands ~2x, not 3x. Fix: apply the delta trick inside the union itself—residual-coded union ≈ 29/64 × 0.84 ≈ 0.38 GB/token → 3.4x, ~4 tok/s. First measure one layer pair's residual entropy given its best L-1 predictor; confirm ≤2 bits before building. Hedge routing precision (0.55) by falling back to full slice when residual exceeds budget.

Compute is the real cap: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s. Use predictive coding with residual gating—predict each routed expert's output from the dense path plus already-computed experts, and skip its matmul when predicted residual norm is below threshold. Skipping ~5 of 10 experts/layer cuts FLOPs 12→~7 GFLOP/token, giving ~7.8 tok/s (~1.7x) on compute alone; layer onto the I/O path only where I/O already clears, landing ~3x+ without dividing by the I/O factor.

The 3x decode target isn't reachable by a database-lens hit-rate trick: routing is already exact, so late materialisation saves nothing, and the real floor is max(I/O, compute) — 1.85 tok/s I/O vs 4.6 tok/s compute. Cheapest first measurement: log per-token read-wait vs compute; if compute ≥70%, stop — the bound is FLOPs, not hit rate, and no cache trick helps. Only cutting FLOPs/token or bytes/token together moves the ceiling.

Prefill is compute-bound, not I/O-bound: ~109 s compute vs ~29 s reads, so overlapping I/O makes the disk bound vanish, not shrink. Issue each layer's ~27 MB expert reads with io_uring O_DIRECT, double-buffered one layer ahead into pinned buffers, so matmul never blocks. TTFT falls from 138 s to ~109 s. Don't assume 311 GFLOP/s batched prefill—measure it; if sustained, compute drops to ~19 s and I/O binds at ~29 s (4.7x). This attacks TTFT only; decode tok/s is unchanged.

Distill the MoE into a dense ~6B student (3.2 GB at 4.3 bits) that fits fully resident in 8 GB, eliminating expert I/O so decode is compute-bound at ~4.6 tok/s; add mixture-of-depths so each token runs half the layers (6 GFLOP/token) to reach ~9.2 tok/s, accepting 2-5 PPL cost and keeping the MoE on disk as fallback.

Use the 0.55 next-layer predictor as a learned-cache admission oracle, but pin only top-confidence predicted experts and never skip experts (skipping changes outputs). At 24 GB: 1.9 GB dense + ~20 GB pinned (29% of 69 GB). Per token, 480 slices = 1.3 GB; predictor turns 0.55 of next-layer misses into hits, so streamed ≈ 1.3×(1−0.55) ≈ 0.59 GB → 0.38 s → 2.6 tok/s; ARC-style ghost-list tuning lifts precision to ~0.7 → 0.39 GB → 0.25 s → 4.0 tok/s, clearing 3x over 1.2 tok/s. Compute stays 4.6 tok/s, so I/O drops below it. Quality cost: none; only cache residency changes. First measurement: 200

Decode is compute-bound: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, and no disk speed fixes that. Add an FPGA co-processor doing int8 expert GEMMs at ~200 GFLOP/s; the CPU keeps dense weights and attention. Offloading the expert matmuls (~10 GFLOP/token) leaves the CPU ~2 GFLOP/token, so aggregate ~165 GFLOP/s clears 3x. I/O must be hidden behind it: 1.3 GB/token ÷ 2.4 GB/s = 0.54 s (~1.8 tok/s floor), so pair with k=8 union (29/64) to reach ~0.24 s (~4 tok/s). Quality: int8 experts cost ~+0.3 ppl. Cheapest first measurement: time one expert slice's int8 GEMM on the FPGA vs the CPU.

At 24 GB, ~21.5 GB caches experts, so I/O unbinds (~0.54 s) and compute binds (~0.22 s) → 4.6 tok/s, ~1.5x over 3 tok/s. ARC/2Q can't help: cross-prompt reuse is 5–21%. The real lever is learned/online caching within a sequence: k=8 consecutive tokens share experts (union 29/64), so group decode loads each slice once → ~0.09 GB/token, I/O ~0.04 s, compute binds at 4.6 tok/s. To clear 3x, add per-layer expert prediction (previous layer predicts next at 0.55) to prefetch the likely set during compute. First measure per-layer expert IDs over 8-token groups: union/64 and predictor hit rate.

Prefill streams all 69 GB once, so attack TTFT via storage, not decode: use a Zoned Namespace SSD with zone-aligned expert blobs (each expert's 3 tensors contiguous in one zone), so the FTL never does read-modify-write or GC during the pass—removing the ~1.5 GB/s cliff and sustaining 2.4 GB/s. That gives 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s = 29 s I/O, overlapped with ~19 s compute → ~29 s TTFT vs ~100 s mmap (3.4x), at zero quality cost. Cheapest test: one layer (1.4 GB) via ZNS zone-aligned O_DIRECT vs mmap, measure sustained GB/s.

TTFT is a 69 GB single-pass I/O problem: treat RAM as L3 for the NVMe L4. Prefill expert-major, streaming each expert slice sequentially into a small ring of 4 MiB-aligned pinned buffers so the core consumes slice n while the prefetcher pulls n+1 (MLP across 480 slices). 69 GB at 5 GB/s ≈ 14 s, overlapped with 6 TFLOP ÷ 311 GFLOP/s ≈ 19 s, gives TTFT ≈ 19 s vs 125–250 s baseline — >3x, lossless. First measure: one 500-token prompt, expert-major with prefetch ring vs 0.9 MB slices; confirm Gen4 sequential rate first.

Make expert bytes come from fast memory, not NVMe: on the 16 GB laptop, pin a per-layer hot expert subset in L3/RAM with SIMD-friendly layout, reserving ~8 GB for dense+KV and ~7 GB for hot experts (~10.6% of slices), and bias routing to them so ~90% of each token's 1.3 GB is resident—cutting NVMe traffic to ~0.13 GB (~54 ms) plus 217 ms compute ≈ 3.7 tok/s. But that's only ~1.5x, not 3x: the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling caps any I/O trick, so this removes the I/O bound but cannot clear 3x—only lowering FLOPs/token can. Quality cost: routing bias slightly changes outputs. Cheapest measurement: ml

Use ARC-style adaptive caching on the actual access sequence, not cross-prompt hot lists: keep the 1.9 GB dense resident plus ~21.5 GB expert slices in a 2Q/ARC cache, and prefetch the next layer's top-scoring expert slices during current-layer compute using the current router logits as Belady-style lookahead. At 0.55 next-layer precision, ~55% of the 1.3 GB/token is prefetched and overlapped, leaving ~0.6 GB demand plus prefetch fitting the 2.4 GB/s budget (~0.54 s/token, ~1.9 tok/s I/O), so compute caps at ~4.6 tok/s — a 1.5–2.3x gain, not 3x, at zero quality cost since routing is unchanged.

Pin 1.9 GB dense plus a 20 GB expert window in 24 GB RAM, lay remaining experts on disk in routing-decision order for sequential 2.4 GB/s streaming, and add ARC-style adaptive replacement to keep the window at ~90% hit, cutting I/O to ~0.05 s and reaching ~3.7 tok/s (compute-bound, ~1.6x). 3x (≥6-12 tok/s) is unreachable since compute caps at 4.6 tok/s. Quality cost ~1-2 pts. First measure: time 480 preads on a reordered 1 GB sample.

Prefill is I/O-bound: 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s vs compute 6 TFLOP ÷ 311 GFLOP/s ≈ 19 s. Cut prefill FLOPs (INT8 expert weights, rank-64 attention) to ~8-11 s, then cut bytes: skip layers with router mass <2% (~25% of layers, ~17 GB less I/O) → ~22 s TTFT, ~2x. 3x is not reachable within these bounds; honest achievable is ~2x. Verify quality via fp32-vs-quantized logit KL < 0.02 on 20 prompts.

Ternary experts cut compute, but I/O still binds: 0.5 GB at 2.4 GB/s is 4.8 tok/s. Coalesce into 4 MiB reads and cache the 42% repeat experts to reach ~6-7 tok/s (~1.5x decode). First measure: quantise one layer, time matmul vs fp16, check perplexity delta.

Cache gate-weighted expert outputs, not weights: per layer, store a rank-8 output codebook (~0.1 MB/expert) built offline; at decode, gate scores pick which experts to materialise, and low-gate experts are answered index-only from the codebook instead of loading 2.7 MB. This removes the compute bound: 60% index-only slices cut FLOPs from 12 to ~5 GFLOP/token (4.6→11 tok/s, 2.4x) and bytes to ~0.5 GB/token, so I/O no longer binds—≥3x total. Cost: ~2-4% perplexity on those slices. First measure: log gate score vs. codebook-vs-exact error per expert to find the threshold giving 60% index-only at

Idle-time prefix prefill alone can't 3x decode; pair it with the same session-aware mechanism on decode: while the user types, pre-warm the exact experts the next prompt's prefix routing selects, pinning each session's 480-slice expert working set. If that pinned set covers ~70% of slices, decode bytes fall from 1.3 GB to ~0.4 GB/token, cutting ~0.83 s to ~0.26 s (1.2→3.9 tok/s, 3.2x), and prefill's 29 s I/O leaves TTFT. Exact, no approximation. Cheapest test: log per-token slice hits from the pinned set on one real session.

Prefill is I/O-bound (69 GB ÷ 1.56 GB/s ≈ 44 s), and the 1.56 vs 2.4 GB/s gap is the sub-4 MiB read tax on 0.9 MB expert tensors. Even fixing it (4 MiB-aligned O_DIRECT io_uring reads → 29 s I/O) plus expert-major streaming and batched compute (19 s) yields TTFT ≈ 29 s vs 44 s: only 1.5x. 3x is not reachable on TTFT from I/O alone; cheapest test is timing 480 sequential 0.9 MB preads vs 4 MiB-aligned O_DIRECT io_uring reads.
