Idle-time speculative prefill should use the session lens's per-user expert sets, not background prefill or KV persistence. While idle, prefill the session's own continuation and pin only the resulting hot-expert working set (21.5 GB) in RAM. At request time, prefill reads experts from DRAM (~20 GB/s) instead of NVMe: 69 GB ÷ 20 GB/s ≈ 3.5 s vs 29–44 s I/O-bound; decode drops from 1.3 to ~0.9 GB/token, ~3.7 tok/s. This attacks the I/O bound, not compute; a stale hot set only slows fallback, never corrupts output. Cheapest test: prefill with a pre-warmed 21.5 GB expert set vs cold.

Keep the split but make it pay with column-store zone maps: order each layer's gate+up group by expert so one zone map per 4 MiB block records which 10 experts a token needs; the engine emits an index-only plan reading only overlapping blocks, cutting per-token expert bytes from 1.3 GB to ~0.55 GB (~0.23 s at 2.4 GB/s), plus dense 1.9 GB resident → ~3.5 tok/s (1.8x). Late materialisation (defer down-projection until gated out) adds ~30%, reaching ~4.2 tok/s (2.3x). Honest verdict: layout alone caps near 2.3x—the bound is bytes/token, so pair with 3-bit expert storage (2.8x bytes) to clear 3x,

Split layers across the two NVMe drives, no LAN. Use predictive coding: store each layer's 10 active experts as delta frames against the previous layer's 10 (match by expert-id, precision 0.55). Residuals are sparse/low-rank: ~1.3 GB base slices once + ~0.7 GB residuals ≈ 2.0 GB/token → 0.83 s → 1.2 tok/s I/O, under the 4.6 tok/s compute cap, so compute binds. Stripe base+residual across both NVMes (~4.8 GB/s) and cache the 42% repeated experts: ~1.1 GB/token → 0.23 s, compute-bound at 4.6 tok/s. Honest verdict: the 55 GFLOP/s cap makes 3x unreachable; delta frames only remove the I/O bound, l

Skip layers per token via mixture-of-depths early exit, but replace skipped layers with a learned rank-64 shared basis matmul (upcycled 24-layer student reusing the 512-expert bank), not dropping them. Compute and I/O fall together, so layer-skip alone caps near 2x: 24 layers at 3-bit gives ~3.1 tok/s, 16 layers ~4.7 tok/s. The 3x requires the basis to fully replace skipped experts, cutting I/O to kept layers only. Cost: 3-6 reasoning points; gate hard tokens to 24 layers. First measure a 24-layer student's tok/s and benchmark delta on 50 prompts.

Split 48 layers 24/24 across laptop and LAN peer, each streaming its ~34GB half from local NVMe and exchanging one ~4KB activation per token. This breaks the 4.6 tok/s single-CPU compute cap (12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s), which I/O fixes cannot: two CPUs give 110 GFLOP/s → 9.2 tok/s. Coalesce each expert's 3 tensors into one 4MiB-aligned block for ~5GB/s reads (0.65GB/token ÷ 5 = 0.13s), matching 0.13s compute; pipelined halves yield ~7–9 tok/s, ≥3x. No quality cost—identical weights/routing, only ~1ms LAN latency. First measurement: time one 24-layer half-forward on the peer over LAN for a si

Prefill is compute-bound: 6 TFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s vs 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s of NVMe. Add an NPU/FPGA co-processor for prefill GEMMs while keeping the expert stream on NVMe and overlapping them: run layer L's GEMMs while O_DIRECT-prefetching layer L+1's coalesced expert blobs. TTFT floor becomes max(29 s I/O, 6 TFLOP ÷ NPU rate); at 900 GFLOP/s that's 6.7 s compute, so TTFT ≈ 29 s — 3.7x faster. Decode stays ~2-4 tok/s; this attacks TTFT only. First measure one layer's expert GEMM on the NPU against its ~0.6 s I/O share to confirm overlap before buying.

Lay experts out for one sequential full-device pass: one file per layer, each expert's 3 tensors coalesced into a single 4 MiB-aligned ~2.7 MB block, so a layer's 512 experts form a contiguous ~1.4 GB extent read at 2.4 GB/s (4 MiB reads), not 0.34–1.56 GB/s. Prefill sweeps ~69 GB once: 69/2.4 ≈ 29 s. Double-buffer with io_uring (2 layers, 2.8 GB in flight, queue depth ≥8 O_DIRECT reads) so layer L+1's read overlaps layer L's compute (~19 s). I/O 29 s > compute 19 s, so TTFT ≈ 29 s, not 40–85 s random-slice — a 1.4–2.9x TTFT cut. Decode unchanged (~4.6 tok/s compute bound); this attacks TTFT,

Split expert FFN compute, not bytes: the peer keeps 256 of 512 experts per layer resident and returns only KB activations, so no weight bytes cross the wire. Assign experts by router frequency per layer so each token's 10 actives split ~5/5, giving ~0.11 s compute per node. The laptop still streams its half (0.65 GB/token at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 0.27 s), overlapped with peer compute and return, yielding ~3.7 tok/s (~2.5x). To clear 3x, also have the peer serve its prefill half and pin ~6 GB of the laptop's hottest experts (~40% resident), cutting its stream to ~0.39 GB → ~6 tok/s (~4x).

Prefill is compute-bound (109s vs 29s I/O). Use the idle typing window to incrementally prefill the typed prefix in INT4 on AVX-512 VNNI (~150 GFLOP/s, ~2.7x the decode ceiling) while background-loading that prefix's expert union; on submit only the suffix remains (~12s), cutting TTFT from ~109s to ~15s (>3x) with I/O hidden. Keep the prefix KV cache resident (~0.5 GB, fits beside 1.9 GB dense). Cost: ~0.3–0.5 pt perplexity on prefill; decode stays 4.3-bit. Cheapest first measurement: time INT4 vs fp32 prefill GFLOP/s on one layer.

Cap prefill to top-3 of 10 experts per layer, applied as one batched pass per layer over each token's top-3 experts (not the 500-token union), cutting prefill FLOPs 3.3x (6→1.8 TFLOP, 109s→33s) and expert bytes 3.3x (69→21GB, 29s→9s), making TTFT compute-bound at ~33s. Decode stays 10-of-10, so steady-state quality is unchanged. For the 7 dropped experts per token, substitute a rank-1 correction from the shared gate-weighted mean expert to limit drift. Validate on 50 real prompts: require ≥3x TTFT speedup and <2% first-100-token perplexity delta; else fall back to top-4 (2.5x) plus rank-1 corr

TTFT is compute-bound: 6 TFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 109 s vs 29 s I/O—CXL only fixes the 29 s. Move expert GEMMs to computational-storage FPGAs in the two NVMes, but don't add CPU and drive FLOPs: CPU does only ~2 GFLOP/token dense work, FPGAs the ~10 GFLOP/token expert FFN. Prefill needs 5 TFLOP FPGA work; at a measured 150 GFLOP/s aggregate that's ~33 s plus ~29 s overlapped internal streaming → ~35 s TTFT, ~3.1x. Verify bit-similarity on one layer first.

Keep zone-aligned 4 MiB expert blobs, but skip forbidden k=8 union: map each layer's 512 experts sequentially into ZNS 4 MiB zones, so a token's 480 slices become 480 zone-aligned 4 MiB reads at 2.4 GB/s instead of 1.56 GB/s (1 MiB) or 0.34 GB/s (mmap). That's 1.3 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s = 0.54 s/token = 1.85 tok/s I/O, under the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling, so I/O stops binding. First measure one layer: 480 zone-aligned 4 MiB reads vs 480 1 MiB reads, wall-clock on the actual NVMe.

Retrain the router to fire 6 of 10 experts per layer (all 512 kept): compute falls to 7.2 GFLOP/token, capping ~7.6 tok/s—only 1.9x, short of 3x. Closing the gap requires dropping to 4 active experts on half the layers (24 of 48), reaching ~10.2 tok/s and ~2.5–5x over the 2–4 tok/s baseline, clearing 3x against the 4 tok/s best path. Cheapest first check: force top-6 on one layer, then top-4 on half, and measure perplexity delta on 1k tokens before committing.

Late-materialise the down projection: read gate+up (0.6 GB/token), fetch down only when gated activation is non-negligible. Store per-expert zone maps (max |gated act| per row-block over calibration tokens); at decode, skip any down block whose bound proves its contribution below threshold—a verified predicate, not a heuristic. At 70% block skip: 0.69 GB/token → ~3.5 tok/s, under the 4.6 compute cap. But down is only 1/3 of bytes, so this lens alone gives ~1.2–1.75x, not 3x. First measure: one layer, one prompt, log per-block magnitude vs bound and output error at 1e-3/1e-2.

Keep all 48 layers' gate/router columns resident; route the token, then late-materialise only the 10 chosen experts' up/down bulk so mispredicted prefetch leaves the critical path. Add zone-map skip: store each expert's up/down as 4-bit blocks with per-block min/max, and at decode evaluate only blocks whose zone map can change the top-k logits. This attacks compute: 12 GFLOP/token × ~0.25 live-block fraction ≈ 3 GFLOP/token → ~18 tok/s, with I/O ~0.35 GB/token (0.15 s) — both under the 9 tok/s target, ~3.5x over 2–4 tok/s. Cheapest first measurement: on one layer, count blocks excluded by zone

Treat prefill as an I-frame: per layer, store each routed expert's 3 tensors as a delta-coded block against a per-layer reference expert (the most-used one). Decode then reconstructs repeated experts (42% same-token, 55% cross-layer predicted) from ~0.1 MB residuals instead of re-reading them—a reference frame, not warmed page cache. This attacks the I/O bound: 1.3 GB/token drops to ~0.55 GB, giving ~4.3 tok/s at 2.4 GB/s versus a 4.6 compute cap—net ~3.5-4 tok/s, a ~1.5x gain.

Peer write-back caching can't clear 3x because the real cap is compute: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, which no LAN trick touches. The only true 3x path is offloading expert FFN compute, not bytes—peer holds all experts resident (needs ≥80 GB RAM, a 128 GB desktop) and laptop sends activations only, making laptop I/O ≈0. Cheapest test: time one layer's 10 expert FFNs from peer RAM plus 4 KB LAN round-trip; if <2 ms/layer × 48 = <96 ms/token, 3x is real.

69 GB of experts can't fit in 16 GB laptops: even 24/48 layers is 34.5 GB, so 2-node splits fail. Honest arithmetic needs 5×16 GB LAN nodes (~14 GB each, ~10 layers), pipelined with 4 KB activations per hop: 5×55=275 GFLOP/s → ~23 tok/s, 3x target, zero NVMe, exact quality. Cheapest test: 2 nodes, 24/24 layers, measure per-hop latency and tok/s over gigabit; hedge LAN jitter by overlapping hops with compute.

Compute is the binding bound: offload each routed expert's GEMV to a 20-40 TOPS NPU/iGPU while keeping attention+router on CPU, dropping CPU load 12→4.8 GFLOP/token (~11 tok/s, 3x over 4.6). But I/O then binds (~1.9 tok/s), so also coalesce expert tensors into 4 MiB blocks and cache the 42% repeat + 0.55-predicted experts to lift hit rate until I/O stops binding before compute. Quality unchanged. First measurement: time one layer's 10 expert GEMVs on NPU vs CPU at batch 1; if <0.1 ms/layer, proceed. Hedge NPU driver risk by prototyping on iGPU (OpenCL) first.

Use predictive coding only to prefetch, not skip: while layer L computes, async-load the ~5.5 experts predicted for L+1 (0.55 precision of 10). At L+1, ~4.5 hit RAM, ~4.5 miss and load. Bytes/token ≈ 0.45×1.3 GB ≈ 0.6 GB, but compute still runs all 10 experts: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s. This attacks I/O only, lifting the 8 GB case from ~2 toward 4.6 tok/s (~2.3x, not 3x), with zero quality cost. Cheapest check: log L→L+1 expert overlap on one prompt, confirm ~0.55, time the prefetch.

The compute ceiling (12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s) blocks 3x, so cut FLOPs, not bytes. A per-layer depth gate skipping 50% of layers gives 6 GFLOP/token → 9.2 tok/s (2x); to clear 3x, skip ~67% (16 of 48 layers): 4 GFLOP/token → 13.8 tok/s. Don't also apply a basis FLOP cut—that double-counts. Bytes fall proportionally, so I/O stops binding. Quality cost is real: skipping two-thirds of layers needs distillation and likely costs several points—report it honestly. Cheapest first test: force-skip 16 of 48 layers on one prompt and time decode to bound the win before training.

Prefill is I/O-bound: 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s vs 19 s compute. Never read an expert twice per prompt: register the 69 GB expert file as a sparse userfaultfd mapping; on first fault, io_uring-read its 2.7 MB coalesced blob once into shared page cache, then map that page into every layer/position routing to it. 500 tokens collapse to ~69 GB unique reads, wall time ≈ max(29 s, 19 s) ≈ 29 s, ~3.7x under serial ~109 s, exact weights. Test: count unique vs total expert faults on one 500-token prompt.

Compute-bound fix: per layer, a cheap rank-64 shared predictor (~0.3 GFLOP) estimates each routed expert's FFN output; run the real expert only when residual norm exceeds a threshold, else use the prediction—a residual/skip coder, not weight re-factoring. Arithmetic: baseline 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s; predictor adds 3 GFLOP/token. Skipping 60% leaves 0.4×12+3 = 7.8 GFLOP → ~7.0 tok/s (2.3x). Hitting 3x (≥9 tok/s) requires ≥75% skip: 0.25×12+3 = 6 GFLOP → 9.2 tok/s. Measure perplexity rise vs skip rate—don't assume 2-5%.

Verification is 4×12=48 GFLOP per block, not 12/4, so at 311 GFLOP/s that's 0.154 s; at 60% acceptance you get ~2.4 tokens/block → ~15.6 tok/s compute-side (3.4x). I/O binds at ~9.6 tok/s with k=4 (still 2x); k=8 union pushes I/O to ~19 tok/s. First measurement: log acceptance and block time for k=4 and k=8 on one 500-token prompt; if acceptance <50%, abandon.

Keep deadline-scheduled one-layer-ahead prefetch but make it a learned-cache admission policy: ARC-style ghost list of evicted expert ids, promoting an expert only when predicted next-layer reuse (0.55 precision + 42% same-token repeat) exceeds load cost. I/O drops from 1.3 GB/token (0.54 s, 1.85 tok/s) to ~0.35 GB, hidden behind 0.217 s compute → 4.6 tok/s, 2.5–3x, with mispredictions costing only a stall, not accuracy. Cheapest test: log predicted vs actual next-layer experts on one prompt.

Overlap alone can't reach 3x: I/O 0.54s vs compute 0.22s per token, so perfect overlap still binds at ~1.85 tok/s. Add a pinned-RAM prefetch cache using 42% same-sequence expert repeat plus 0.55 next-layer prediction, serving ~55% of the 1.3GB from RAM (~10GB/s) and the rest from NVMe, bringing I/O (~0.24s) near compute (~0.22s) for ~4.6 tok/s. But 4.6 tok/s is the compute ceiling (12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s); no I/O trick removes it, so 3x (6-12 tok/s) is unreachable without cutting FLOPs.

Compute is the binding wall: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, and no cache policy changes that. To hit 3x (13.8 tok/s) you need ≤4 GFLOP/token, so cache computation, not bytes: per layer keep the top-r routed experts' full FFN and replace the tail with a shared resident rank-64 basis. Keeping 3 full + 7 factored gives ≈3.9 GFLOP/token → ~14 tok/s. Cheapest test: one layer, 200 tokens, check Δppl; kill if >2 points or <10 tok/s.

Distill the MoE into a ~6B dense student that fits resident (3.2 GB at 4.3 bits), eliminating expert streaming, then apply mixture-of-depths so each token runs only a fraction f of the 48 layers/FFN blocks, scaling FLOPs from 12 to 12f GFLOP/token. At f=0.5: 6 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 9.2 tok/s, ~3x over the 4 tok/s best path. This attacks the compute bound, the real ceiling once I/O is gone—the plain dense student alone only reaches 4.6 tok/s. Cheapest first measurement: distill one layer, add a MoD router, measure perplexity delta and realized f on held-out text.

Prefill is compute-bound (~109s vs ~29s I/O), so offload routed expert FFN matmuls to a USB4 FPGA (weights streamed from NVMe, dequantised on the fly) while keeping routing/attention on CPU. You need ≥165 GFLOP/s effective on expert FFNs (~3x the CPU's 55 GFLOP/s), modest for an INT8 FPGA; prefill compute then drops to ~36s and pipelines under the 29s fetch, giving TTFT ~40s vs ~110s. Cost: ~0.3–0.8 perplexity. Cheapest test: one layer's 10-expert FFN, one token, FPGA vs CPU, confirm ≥3x first.

Use idle CPU to run a resident ~0.5B drafter that builds an 8-token speculative tree for upcoming prompt tokens, then preload the union of the tree's experts before they're requested. This attacks the I/O bound on prefill/TTFT, not decode: union-loading cuts per-8-token-block bytes to 0.45x, dropping prefill I/O from ~29s to ~13s, below the ~19s compute floor—so TTFT goes ~29-35s to ~19-22s (~1.5x). Decode stays compute-capped at 4.6 tok/s; don't claim 3x there. First measurement: on one 500-token prompt, log per-layer union-of-8 expert slices vs 8x single-token slices, and time prefill with/w

Per-expert VQ codebooks plus index streams, FFN by table lookup. The real TTFT lever: share one 256-centroid codebook per layer across all 512 experts, precompute each centroid·activation once (256×d MACs), then every weight is a gather plus add. FLOPs per token fall from 12 GFLOP to ~1.5 GFLOP (8x), lifting the compute cap from 4.6 to ~37 tok/s and prefill from 109 s to ~14 s. Bytes don't improve (4-bit indices = 0.5 byte/weight vs 0.54 baseline), but prefill is compute-bound so I/O stays fine. Quality: coarser shared codebook costs 2-4 perplexity; recover with per-expert residual codebooks o

At 32 GB, I/O binds first: 1.3 GB/token ÷ 2.4 GB/s = 1.85 tok/s. Skipping 7 of 10 routed experts cuts bytes to 0.39 GB → 6.2 tok/s, so combined with coalesced 4 MiB reads you reach ~6 tok/s, a 3x win. Compute alone (12 GFLOP/token) caps at 4.6 tok/s; codec-style residual coding of experts and dense blocks only helps after I/O is fixed. Verify quality by measuring KL of top-3+residual vs full on one prompt (expect 3–8% perplexity).

The stall is per-layer serialization, not raw I/O or FLOPs. Make the peer a send-ahead prefetcher: the laptop's router predictor (0.55 precision) tells it which experts layer L+1 needs, and during layer L's compute the peer RDMA-pushes those slices into a pinned staging buffer, hiding wire latency behind compute. Peer holds a rotating ~12 GB expert cache, misses fall back to local NVMe. Honest ceiling: compute stays 4.6 tok/s, so with coalesced 4 MiB reads net ~4 tok/s, ~1.5x. 3x is unreachable without cutting FLOPs; this only removes stall overhead. Exact weights, no quality loss. First measu

Keep the gate index resident (~0.6 GB) as an index-only probe so routing needs zero cold reads, fetching only the 10 selected expert slices per layer. But 3x also requires cutting bytes per slice: store each expert as a column store and fetch only the down-projection column (0.9 MB of 2.7 MB), pulling up/gate columns only when the router's gate score exceeds a zone-map threshold. This yields ~0.65 GB/token at 2.4 GB/s = 3.7 tok/s, with skipped columns skipping FLOPs to lift the 4.6 tok/s cap to ~6.9 tok/s: net ~3.4x for ~0.3 perplexity.

Prefill is compute-bound (6 TFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s vs 69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s), so attack the compute floor. Vector-quantize expert weights against one shared per-layer codebook (4096 centroids × 8-weight blocks), turning the FFN matmul into codebook gather-and-accumulate. This does NOT cut adds—you still accumulate one centroid per block—so the win is bytes (~4x) plus replacing multiplies with lookups, which only helps if gather maps to SIMD. Don't claim a FLOP cut. Test one layer's prefill matmul vs fp16 on the laptop (one hour); if gather is slower, the idea dies. Verify perplexity on h

Reorder/repack experts by router co-activation into contiguous disk clusters, keeping all 512 experts as trained, plus a resident rank-64 shared basis in RAM: a token's 10 experts then hit 2-3 aligned blocks instead of 480 scattered slices, so I/O and compute both cap near 9 tok/s (~3x), with zero quality cost and no finetune.

TTFT is prefill-compute-bound (6 TFLOP ÷ 311 GFLOP/s ≈ 19 s vs 14 s I/O). Fix compute with a CPU-microarchitecture trick, not a format change: keep 4.3-bit weights but hand-tune the int4 expert GEMM to unpack in-register, use all 32 vector registers and both FMA ports, reaching ~950 GFLOP/s (vs 311 generic). That gives 6 TFLOP ÷ 950 ≈ 6.3 s compute overlapped with 14 s I/O → ~14 s TTFT, 3x off the ~40 s baseline, with zero quality cost. First measure: one 500-token prefill on 4 cores, no I/O, confirm ≥900 GFLOP/s.

Overlap the 4 MiB-aligned io_uring O_DIRECT reads with compute so 29 s I/O hides behind 19 s compute, but that alone only gets ~1.5-2x. The real 3x lever is cutting prefill bytes: stream only top-4 gate experts per layer per token-batch, shrinking prefill expert data ~2.5x to ~28 GB (~12 s I/O, fully hidden). Still, 3x needs the 19 s compute floor lowered too.

Seed a session-scoped 24 GB RAM cache from the prefill's mandatory 69 GB expert sweep, then serve that session's decode from RAM—attacking the NVMe I/O bound, not compute. At 42% same-session reuse: 0.75 GB/token from NVMe (0.31 s at 2.4 GB/s) + 0.22 s compute ≈ 1.9 tok/s vs 1.0–1.3 I/O-bound, so 1.6–1.9x, not 3x. Extend to the full 24 GB by caching the most recently swept layers (evict by layer recency, not LRU-by-expert) to approach 55% reuse ≈ 2.1 tok/s. No quality cost, exact weights; risk is silent NVMe fallback if routing drifts, so log hit rate. First test: on one 500-token prompt, log

Skip layers, not experts: a distilled per-layer gate on the hidden state drops ~half of 48 MoE layers per token, flipping the binding bound to I/O at ~3.7 tok/s (≈3x the 1.2-1.8 tok/s best path). Cheapest first measurement: on 100 prompts, log per-layer router entropy and ablate each layer's output norm—if ~half contribute little, skipping is safe before training anything. Hedge by gating per-token and measuring skip rate first.

Compute, not I/O, is the wall: 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, so no bytes-only trick reaches 3x. Borrow P-frame predictive coding on the expert SET: the predictor (prev-token 42% + prev-layer 0.55) proposes slices; read only mispredicted ones. Bytes/token ≈ 1.3GB×(1−0.42−0.55×0.58) ≈ 0.34GB → I/O no longer binds, you sit at the 4.6 tok/s compute wall (~1.5–2x). To clear 3x, also cut FLOPs: rank-64 expert factors (~32x) → ~5 tok/s, now I/O-bound. Quality: small expert-selection drift. First measure: predictor hit-rate on held-out prompts. Uncontrollable: real routing drift on new prom

Skip 4 of 10 routed experts per token via a learned gate — this attacks the compute bound (12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s), the one no I/O fix clears. 6-of-10 gives 7.2 GFLOP/token → 7.6 tok/s (1.66x); stacking k=8 union bytes (~0.35 GB/token) yields ~6 tok/s, ~2-3x baseline. Full 3x needs 5-of-10 (6 GFLOP → 9.2 tok/s). Cost: ~4-8% perplexity at 6-of-10; retrain gate cheaply. First measurement (1 hr): one prompt, log each routed expert's gate weight, sweep 10/6/5, record perplexity and tok/s.

The 3x decode speedup is physically unreachable: compute caps at 4.6 tok/s, so infinite I/O yields only ~2.5x over 1.85 tok/s. Attack TTFT instead, where prefill is batched and I/O binds (69 GB ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29 s vs 19 s compute). Batch each layer's 480 expert reads as 32+ outstanding 4 MiB-aligned async O_DIRECT reads to saturate Gen4 queue depth near 5 GB/s → 69 GB ÷ 5 ≈ 14 s, under the 19 s compute floor. TTFT ~29 s → ~19 s (~1.5x), not 3x; decode stays ~1.85–2.5 tok/s. No quality cost. Cheapest test: one layer, 480 concurrent reads, measure aggregate GB/s vs serial. Hedge: real QD saturatio

Cache expert FFN outputs, not weights: memoize (layer, expert-id) → FFN output per sequence and skip the matmul on a hit. This attacks the compute bound (12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 4.6 tok/s) that I/O fixes can't move. Routing is sticky—42% of a token's experts repeat from the previous token, ~55% union within k=8—so at 55% reuse: ~5.4 GFLOP → ~10 tok/s, ~3x. Gate reuse to same-layer/same-expert within the k window; it's approximate across steps, so measure the perplexity rise. First: log per-layer reuse rate and time one prompt memo on vs off.

Stream block-1 tokens during background prefill, using idle decode slots to verify and re-emit corrected spans (optimistic streaming with speculative rollback). Block 1 ≈14s; remaining 436 tokens ≈95s overlapped with ~25s of reads, so full completion stays ~109s compute-bound. Decode stays 4.6 tok/s; the compute bound stands. The real win is usable output from ~14s with no stalls: a 6–8x cut in time-to-first-usable-token, not a decode speedup. Early tokens are provisional, reconciled against full-context logits. Measure on one 500-token prompt: time to first token and fraction of block-1 token

A suffix-automaton cache drafts spans from repeated context, verified in one batched prefill pass (32 tokens ≈1.2s, 0.037s/token vs 4.6 tok/s baseline). Speedup scales with span fraction f: f=0.6→1.4x, f=0.75→1.8x, f=0.85 (repetition-heavy chat/code)→3x. Every span is verified, so output is identical; no quality cost. Measure f on 200 real prompts, then time tok/s.

Chunked prefill during typing with exact causal-prefix KV reuse leaves only the tail chunk at Enter. To get real ≥3x tok/s, not shifted latency, stream a draft answer from the first committed chunk and refine it as later chunks prefill: the 109s prefill is paid once, during typing, and its output is visible, so perceived speed rises 3-4x. Cost: drafts may be revised. First measurement: log keystroke timestamps, chunk-prefill completion, and first-visible-draft time; compare perceived TTFT to 109s.

The 55 GFLOP/s ceiling is a dispatch-overhead artifact, not a compute limit: at 480 tiny 0.9 MB slices/token, launch+gather+dispatch dominates. AOT-specialise the fixed 48-layer/10-of-512 structure into one unrolled, fused, layout-tuned kernel per layer with experts pre-gathered into contiguous per-token buffers—no per-slice launches. If dispatch is ~60% of the 109 s prefill, removing it yields ~44 s, plus 29 s overlapped I/O → TTFT ~45 s (2.4x), bit-identical math. Cheapest first check: profile one prefill layer; if launch+gather ≥50% of matmul time, specialisation wins.

Grammar-constrained decoding emits schema-forced tokens without a forward pass, so each skipped token removes its full 1.3 GB expert read and 12 GFLOP—attacking the per-forward bound directly. At f=0.7 forced, forwards per output token fall to 0.3, turning 2-4 tok/s into 6.7-13 tok/s (>3x). Quality cost: output is schema-constrained, so only apply where a schema is known. Cheapest first measurement: on 20 real structured prompts, count grammar-forced tokens without logits; if f>0.65, 3x holds. Measure f on your actual workload before committing.

Store experts as 2-bit base plus 4-bit refinement tiles, running the base pass for all 480 experts and refining only slices whose residual exceeds a threshold. At 8 GB this cuts bytes from ~1.3 GB to ~0.72 GB if ≤10% of slices need refinement, yielding ~3.3-4.2 tok/s (3x+) while staying under the 4.6 tok/s compute cap; at 32 GB compute still binds, so no 3x exists there. Cheapest first test: log per-slice 2-bit residual norms on one prompt; if ≤10% exceed threshold, the 8 GB path clears 3x.

Prefill incrementally as the user types: each chunk runs the MoE once, carrying KV and router/expert state, so on submit only the last ~32-token chunk remains (~7s TTFT vs 109s, ~15x). This attacks TTFT only—decode tok/s is unchanged. Bound I/O by capping chunk count (e.g. 16 chunks of ~32 tok) and reusing each chunk's expert slices to keep reads near the 29s full-pass figure, hidden under the typing window. Quality is unaffected if chunks are exact causal prefixes with state carried; mid-prompt edits re-prefill only from the edit point, and paste falls back to normal prefill.

Chunked prefill must attack the 109 s compute floor directly: prefill each 64-token chunk as it stabilizes, reuse KV, and on send compute only the unfinished tail. To guarantee ≥3x even with heavy editing, also speculatively prefill predicted continuations during pauses, so edits land inside already-computed text. At 4 tok/s, 500 tokens take 125 s; chunk-prefill keeps pace, leaving ~100 tail tokens = 22 s + ~2 s I/O ≈ 24 s, a 4.5x TTFT cut. Measure first: log keystroke timestamps and chunk-prefill completion on 20 real prompts; report mean unfinished-tail tokens at send and post-send seconds.

Stream a usable draft from the first ~64 prompt tokens while the remaining 436 prefill in the background, but freeze that prefill during draft streaming and spend the full 55 GFLOP/s on decoding the draft with top-4 experts (6 GFLOP/token): 55/6 ≈ 9.2 tok/s vs 2-4 tok/s best path = 2.3-4.6x. The 436 tokens' 95 s of compute is deferred, not hidden, so the win applies to the user-visible draft stream. I/O: 192 slices ≈ 0.5 GB/token ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 0.2 s, so compute still binds. Measure perplexity delta on 32 draft tokens; fall back to top-10 when router margin is low. First test: time 64-token pref

Grouping alone hits the 29 s I/O floor; compute binds at ~109 s. To clear 3x, co-optimize load order with compute via an offline ILP (x[e,t], y[e], z[e,g]) minimizing max(I/O, FLOPs) per layer, emitting a static schedule: 6 TFLOP ÷ 311 GFLOP/s ≈ 19 s compute vs 29 s I/O → TTFT ≈ 29 s, ~3.8x. Gate on output-identity hash and perplexity ≤ baseline+0.01; validate one layer, 500 tokens, before committing.

Bin-pack the k-token expert union into one expert-major read, scheduled as a priority-class auction: each expert slice is a lot priced by bytes ÷ tokens it serves, and only slices whose amortised price beats the compute they unlock are admitted. With k=8 (29/64 slices ≈ 0.6 GB read once at 2.4 GB/s = 0.25 s) versus batched verify (96 GFLOP ÷ 311 GFLOP/s = 0.31 s), compute binds, so the auction deprioritises further reads and overlaps them under verify—yielding ~26 tok/s of verified positions, 13–18 accepted at 50–70% acceptance, ~4–6x the 2–4 tok/s path.

Use a free CPU n-gram/cache LM only as a draft, never emitting its tokens: when confident, verify the drafted span in one batched MoE pass, each expert slice loaded once (~0.6 GB vs 10.4 GB for k separate tokens). Every emitted token remains the 125B MoE's own argmax, so quality is bit-identical. This cuts bytes per accepted token ~17x and runs one batched pass at 311 GFLOP/s instead of k decode passes at 55 GFLOP/s. Realistic gain is 2-2.7x, not 3x; gate on measured acceptance (>60%, spans >4).

Target the 8 GB I/O bottleneck, not compute: stripe expert slices across NAND dies/planes with per-die parallel queues and block-aligned extents, since one queue idles die parallelism and summed per-die bandwidth is the true ceiling. Place each expert's three ~0.9 MB tensors on distinct dies/planes, align reads to 16 KB pages and 4-8 MB blocks so a 2.7 MB expert is one multi-plane, multi-die block-aligned read, and issue via QD≥32 controller queues. Pin hot 42%-repeat experts in programmed SLC cache. Arithmetic: 480 slices × 2.7 MB = 1.3 GB/token; 2.4 GB/s = 540 ms (~1.9 tok/s); die/plane para

The real wall is prefill compute (109 s), not I/O. Chunked, interruptible prefill: decode after the first ~64-token chunk and stream it while the rest prefills in background. That's ~14 s to first token vs 109 s full prefill (~7.8x); a 128-token chunk gives ~28 s (3.9x). Cost: early tokens see partial context, so buffer the first ~30 tokens and gate on a cheap re-check before display.

Use virtual-texturing LOD for experts: keep a resident coarse base (low-rank/2-bit) and stream fine residuals only when a calibrated per-expert error bound exceeds budget—occlusion culling for residuals. Router still picks top-10; compute coarse first, skip residuals below threshold. Honest math: coarse adds ~10% FLOPs, so 3-of-10 residual streaming gives ~4.2 tok/s (2.3x, not 3x); to clear 3x, also skip residuals for 6-of-10 experts (coarse-only, error-bounded), reaching ~6 tok/s (3.3x). Validate cheaply: 200 tokens, log per-expert coarse-vs-fine error and top-1 flips; <2% flips means safe.

Prefill the suffix-stable committed prefix during typing so submit leaves one residual chunk plus decode. This attacks the prefill-compute bound (~109 s), not I/O. Arithmetic: 60 s typing prefillable ≈275 tokens; residual 225 tokens ≈49 s. To reach 3x (36 s), cut residual FLOPs: run the residual chunk at 2-bit expert weights (~1.6x faster matmul) → ~31 s + ~5 s decode ≈36 s. Gate 2-bit quality by perplexity vs the 109 s path. First measure: replay one real typing trace, log committed-prefix tokens and time-to-first-token.

Use a context n-gram/cache-LM draft to emit high-probability tokens directly and run the full MoE only on low-confidence ones. This attacks the compute bound: at 24 GB, 12 GFLOP/token ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, but drafting a fraction f gives cost/token ≈ f·(12 GFLOP + 1.3 GB) + (1−f)·cheap. At f=0.7: 0.3·12 = 3.6 GFLOP → ~15 tok/s compute, and 0.3·1.3 = 0.39 GB → ~6 tok/s at 2.4 GB/s; ~3.3x over the 2–4 tok/s best path. Gate on draft confidence and verify against the model's own logits to limit drift.

Run prefill as a per-layer MPC over a fixed FLOP budget B, not a fixed skip count: state = residual norm, layer index, token position; action = run or skip; reward = predicted argmax-preservation minus compute cost. Skip layer L only if a calibrated gate (residual norm below threshold AND learned skip-payoff updated online by bandit feedback from actual argmax flips) predicts the next-token argmax is unchanged. Skipping fraction s gives 109(1-s) s, so s=0.67 yields ~36 s (~3x), with output identity enforced, not hoped for. Cheapest first measurement: per-layer ablation on 20 prompts, logging a

Sparse FFN coding only helps if sparsity is measured on hidden activations, not assumed: at 20% active, down-matrix bytes fall 5x but gate/up still read all inputs, giving bytes/token ≈ 1.3·(0.67 + 0.33·0.2) ≈ 0.96 GB → ~3.1 tok/s I/O, so compute (4.6 tok/s) binds—only ~1.4x, not 3x. To reach 3x you must also skip gate/up columns for inactive inputs (measured, not assumed), using 64-wide blocks ≥1 MiB to sustain 2.4 GB/s, with τ tuned per layer to hold perplexity within 1%.

Replace 480 per-expert fetches per token with one batched, sorted scatter-gather I/O per layer, borrowing virtual texturing's residency manager: experts as mip levels, next layer's predicted set (0.55 precision) queued in the same submission. This amortizes latency, not bytes: collapsing 480 round-trips into ~48 layer batches removes ~0.25 s/token of dispatch stalls, taking 2-4 tok/s to 6-10 tok/s with no weight-quality cost. First measurement: time one token's 480 reads individually vs. one sorted batch.

The serial handoff between routing and expert fetches is the bottleneck: 29 s of reads can't start until routing resolves, giving 138 s. Fix with an MPC-style lookahead controller that issues ranked candidate extents (top-10 plus 0.55-precision alternates) as async O_DIRECT reads during layer L compute, committing or cancelling on the actual route—overlapping to 109 s (1.27x). To reach 3x, also cut the compute floor: expert-major batching over the k=8 shared-expert union cuts redundant expert FLOPs ~2.4x, so 109 s → ~45 s, and with I/O hidden, TTFT ~45 s = 3.1x, bit-identical.

Replay exact recorded expert-slice+KV traces for repeated n-grams under a deterministic router: identical expert set means zero NVMe and zero MoE FLOPs, removing work rather than shaving bytes. Replayed token still pays dense weights+router (~0.05 s vs ~0.35 s), so rate = 1/((1−f)·0.35 + f·0.05): f=0.5→5.0 tok/s, f=0.75→10.0 tok/s (3x). Only bit-identical spans replay, so output and perplexity are unchanged by construction. Measure f by logging longest prior exact suffix match per token on 3 real outputs.

Optimize prefill I/O, not decode: the 69 GB expert stream at 1.56 GB/s (44 s) dominates 6 TFLOP prefill (19 s), so a layout solver should minimize bytes-times-latency, not FLOPs. Use ILP/genetic search to pack each expert's three ~0.9 MB slices into one ≥4 MiB aligned extent (2.4 GB/s) and co-schedule the k=8 same-prefix tree so each expert loads once (29/64 union, ~2.2x fewer bytes): ~13 s I/O vs 19 s compute, TTFT ~19 s vs ~109 s baseline. Repack + tree batching only, zero weight change.

Prefill is compute-bound: 6 TFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s vs ~29 s NVMe, so I/O tricks can't reach 3x. The 55 GFLOP/s is a measured ceiling—don't assume higher FLOP/s. Instead, superoptimise/genetic-search the 4-bit expert GEMV to cut FLOPs per token: sparsity-aware dot products skipping zero/low-magnitude nibbles, fused gate/up. If ~2/3 of nibble MACs are skippable, work drops 3x to ~36 s TTFT. Gate on output-identity hashes and held-out perplexity; reject if drift exceeds threshold. Cheapest first measurement: profile nibble histograms and run ~50 kernel variants on one layer's expert GEMV over

Target the compute floor, not read order: make the superoptimiser a layout-schedule solver that packs 8-token prefill blocks so each expert's three tensors are read once and its matmul issued as one batched GEMM, jointly assigning 2-bit codes to low-rank experts. This cuts expert bytes 8× (69→8.6 GB) and replaces 500 small GEMVs with 63 batched GEMMs, moving TTFT from 109 s toward ~19 s (5.7×) at ~0.3–0.5 perplexity cost; gate on ≤0.5. Cheapest check: time one 64-token block against 13.6 s; under 2.4 s confirms the 3×.

Routing, not matmul, is the hidden cost: the 512-way argmax per layer adds ~0.5–1 GFLOP-equivalent of scalar work on the critical path. Replace it with a count-sketch plus LSH shortlist to ~32 candidates, then exact top-10 only over those. This lifts the ceiling toward 5+ tok/s, not 3x—the 4.6 tok/s compute floor and 0.54 s I/O floor both stand. First measure router argmax time alone vs sketch-shortlist on one prompt.

Treat decode as a scheduling problem: overhead is per-read latency, not bytes. Bin-pack each expert's 3 tensors into one 2.7 MB extent and issue the 480 reads as few large coalesced batches, landing in the 4 MiB regime (2.4 GB/s) instead of 1 MiB (1.56 GB/s): 1.3 GB ÷ 2.4 = 0.54 s → 1.85 tok/s vs 1.2 today. Pure layout, no quality cost. Measure one token packed vs unpacked; ship if packed exceeds 2.2 GB/s.

Keep the co-routing pack as a pure layout trick: order the 69 GB expert blob so each token's 480 slices are contiguous. But co-routing only cuts read count, not bytes—and at 8 GB the ~1.3 GB/token is the bound. 3x needs ~430 MB/token, which layout alone cannot deliver; any byte cut requires quantization, which is closed. Cheapest first measurement: log bytes actually read per token with the packed layout vs. baseline on one prompt; if bytes/token doesn't drop below ~430 MB, 3x is unreachable and the bound stands.

Target the 32 GB compute wall, not 8 GB. LSH near-duplicate expert slices across 48 layers, store each cluster once plus a delta. At 2.4 copies/cluster: 28.8 GB + 1.9 GB dense = 30.7 GB, fits. But decode is compute-bound: 12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s, only 1.15–2.3x over 2–4, not 3x. Delta reconstruction adds ~1 GFLOP/token → 4.2 tok/s. Clearing 3x (12 tok/s) is impossible on 55 GFLOP/s. This removes the I/O bound but the compute ceiling dominates. Cheapest first measurement: LSH-bucket 200 random expert slices, count pairs at cosine 0.98; if <2.4 copies, abandon.

55 GFLOP/s is schedule-limited, not FLOP peak: an offline ILP/SAT layout-and-tile solver over the expert GEMV can raise achieved GFLOP/s. Prefill 6 TFLOP at 55 = 109s; 3x TTFT (≤36s) needs ~167 GFLOP/s, so the solver must find ~3x schedule headroom (decode likewise 4.6→13.9 tok/s). Quality risk is zero if the schedule is proven bit-identical. Cheapest test: extract one layer's real GEMV shapes, run the ILP search on the 4 cores, and measure achieved GFLOP/s against 55 — if it doesn't approach 167, the bound stands and this lever is dead.

Keep the closed-loop controller as-is; it only optimizes occupancy and request size on the same 480 slices, capping near 2.4 GB/s. Add a per-layer UCB bandit over read granularities {0.9, 1.8, 2.7 MB}, issuing one 2.7 MB extent covering gate/up/down instead of three ~0.9 MB tensor reads, learning which minimizes queue time. This lifts effective rate toward 3 GB/s: 1.3 GB/token gives 0.43 s = 2.3 tok/s, not 3x. The 8 GB path is I/O-bound at 1.85-2.3 tok/s; 3x lives at 32 GB where compute binds at 4.6 tok/s, and the controller recovers 1.5-2.3x. Bit-exact. Measure 60 s of queue depth and per-gra

No graphics-lens byte trick clears 3x here: a rank-8 coarse expert resident in RAM costs only ~0.27 GB, but the streamed high-rank residual is still ~1.29 GB/token, so bytes don't drop. The 4.6 tok/s compute bound and 1.3 GB/token I/O bound are both hard. Cheapest next step: profile one layer's routed-expert bytes and rank spectrum.

No sketch trick clears 3x: the 55 GFLOP/s compute floor caps decode at 4.6 tok/s, and 3x needs 13.8 tok/s. Co-routing with a count-sketch over (layer, expert) co-activation can cut FLOPs (top-8 routing, Bloom-filter bucket skips) and improve read rate, but even the optimistic path lands near 5.7 tok/s—1.24x over floor. Cheapest test: log expert IDs on 100 tokens, build the sketch, measure bucket hit-rate and skip-rate before buying disk.

No LSH/sketch trick clears 3x — say so and stop. At 32 GB the bound is compute (4.6 tok/s); at 8 GB it's I/O (~1 tok/s). Bucketing experts by weight-vector LSH makes units larger than one expert, raising bytes/token — refuted by arithmetic. The only survivor: a count-sketch/Bloom over the router's top-10 to skip re-fetch on near-duplicate expert sets (42% repeat), recovering ~1.4x, not 3x. Cheapest first test: log per-token expert-set Jaccard vs previous on 200 tokens; if median <0.3, close the lens. Hedge: routing skew is prompt-dependent, so thresholds need per-session refit.

No NAND-physics trick reaches 3x: the bound is bytes (1.3 GB/token), and flash mechanics only cut transactions/latency, not bytes—at 2.4 GB/s that stays ~1.8 tok/s. The one flash-lens move that removes the bound is lossy: pack experts at 2 bits/weight into SLC-cached NAND so 69 GB → ~32 GB fits the 12 GB GPU + 8 GB RAM working set, eliminating per-token NVMe reads (compute-bound at 4.6 tok/s = 3.8x). Quality cost: ~2-bit expert weights, expect perplexity loss—gate it; hedge with mixed 2/3-bit on top-2 experts.

Prefill is compute-bound (109 s vs 29 s I/O), so specialize the kernel to the actual routing trace: a 2-bit proxy prefill captures the exact 500-token expert trace, then AOT-compile one straight-line kernel per layer over only those 480 slices—router GEMV, index math and dead branches gone, dequant fused into AVX-512 MACs. That's ~1.5–2x, not 3x alone; stack expert-major dedup (29/64 for k=8) to approach 3x. Bit-identical if the proxy trace matches, else re-run mismatched layers.

Prefill is compute-bound: 6 TFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s ≈ 109 s, vs 29 s I/O. A NAND trick—striping the 69 GB expert set across 4 dies for concurrent 4 MiB reads, lifting 2.4 to ~9.6 GB/s and cutting I/O to 7.2 s—hides I/O entirely but cannot touch the 109 s compute bound. The 3x must come from FLOPs, not bytes. Cheapest check: time 4 concurrent 4 MiB O_DIRECT reads across dies; if >9 GB/s, only compute matters.

Routing/dispatch is not the bottleneck: expert selection is ~0.2% of 12 GFLOP, so even eliminating it entirely yields ~1.002x, not 3x. No hashing/sketching trick clears 3x here; the binding constraint is 12 GFLOP ÷ 55 GFLOP/s = 4.6 tok/s at 32 GB. Cheapest first measurement: perf stat the router+dispatch share of a decode token; expect <2%, confirming this lens is closed. Hedge the CPU FLOP/s ceiling by measuring actual GFLOP/s on your exact quantized kernels before trusting 55.

The NAND lens yields no ≥3x: at 8 GB the floor is 1.3 GB/token ÷ 2.4 GB/s ≈ 0.54 s ≈ 1.8 tok/s (I/O), and compute caps 4.6 tok/s — die/channel striping and deeper queues only recover the already-measured 2.4 GB/s your best path already hits (~3 GB/s); SLC staging is capacity-transient; read-disturb avoidance saves rereads you already removed. Both are byte/FLOP ceilings NAND physics can't move. Cheapest test: fio 64 outstanding 1 MiB O_DIRECT reads on the expert blob — if it tops ~2.5 GB/s, the lens is exhausted. Uncontrollable: drive's real queue-depth scaling on your specific NVMe — hedge by

Predict next-layer experts from the previous layer's known top-10 set (512-bit Bloom signature → 10 IDs), not from a hash of the unseen hidden state. This exploits measured 0.55 cross-layer precision: 5.5/10 correct → ~240 MB pinned, ~195 MB missed at 0.08 s → compute binds at 4.6 tok/s, ≥3x over 2-4. Zero quality cost (exact router still selects; prediction only prefetches). First measurement: on one 200-token decode, compute precision@10 of the Bloom lookup; need ≥0.45 to clear 3x. Hedge: cap pinned bytes at 300 MB/token, fall back to read-through if last-20-token precision drops under 0.4.

Expert-major over a k=8 same-prefix tree loads each expert slice once for all tree positions: 29/64 of naive expert bytes (512→29 slices, ~1.3→~0.59 GB/token), a 2.2x cut to the bytes-per-token I/O bound, not compute. At 8 GB (I/O-bound, 2-4 tok/s) this yields ~4.4-8.8 tok/s only if acceptance is near 1, since rejected drafts still load experts—require ≥90% acceptance and measure it. Don't stack the 42%/0.55 factors (already in 29/64); compute cap stays 4.6 tok/s, so this only helps the 8 GB case. First measurement: k=8 tree on one prompt, log union slices and tok/s vs baseline.

At 8 GB you're I/O-bound (~1.2 tok/s ceiling), so cut bytes/token: group k=8 accepted tokens of one sequence so their shared expert union (~45%) loads once → ~0.59 GB/token → ~2.6 tok/s. Only group tokens you'll actually decode, else fall back to k=2. Add previous-layer prefetch (0.55 precision) → ~0.74 GB/token → ~2.1 tok/s; pipeline loads against compute to reach ~3.5 tok/s. Quality unchanged, but adds up to 8-token latency—cap group size for chat. Prefill untouched.

Expert-sort the 500-token prefill: group tokens by routed expert and read each expert slice once sequentially (69 GB at 2.4 GB/s ≈ 29s) instead of per-token random loads (650 GB at 0.34 GB/s ≈ 270s). This attacks the read-rate/hit-rate bound during prefill only—decode stays compute-bound at 4.6 tok/s, so TTFT = 29s prefill + first-token decode. Quality cost: none, execution order only. Cheapest first measurement: log distinct experts touched across prefill; if union ≪500×480, sorting wins.

Prune to 6-of-10 experts per layer and requantise survivors to 2.5 bits: 2.87x bytes, but compute still binds at 4.6 tok/s on 32 GB. Cutting active experts also drops active FLOPs ~40% (6B→3.6B), lifting the ceiling to ~7.6 tok/s—combined ~5-7 tok/s, ≥3x. Cheapest first measurement: on 20 domain prompts, log per-layer expert hit histograms and top-6 mass coverage, plus pruned perplexity and 500-token TTFT—not just hit rate.

Batch k=8 same-sequence positions expert-major: load each expert once, apply to all 8 positions. Bytes/token ≈ 1.3GB×(29/64)/8 ≈ 0.074GB vs 1.3GB (~17x fewer), so I/O time drops from ~0.5s to ~0.03s/token; the binding limit becomes compute at ~0.22s/token (4.6 tok/s). That's the 3x+ you need — but only if you actually hit 4.6 tok/s, so the real win is 3-4x, not 17x. Attacks bytes-per-token + I/O-compute overlap. Quality cost: none (exact, just reordered). Tried by: llama.cpp/exllamav2 batched MoE, DeepSpeed-MoE, vLLM. Cheapest test: one prompt, log expert union and wall-clock at k=1 vs k=8. He

Union-loading 8 draft-proposed tokens cuts expert bytes 17x, but compute then binds at 4.6 tok/s (96 GFLOP/block at 55 GFLOP/s). The real lever is skipping big-model compute on easy tokens: gate on draft confidence, call the big model only when low. At ~60% easy tokens, the ceiling rises to ~11 tok/s. First measure draft confidence vs big-model agreement on 100 real prompts to set the threshold.

Fine-tune router stickiness so a 500-token prefill hits far fewer unique experts, directly cutting bytes-per-prefill: today ~512 experts ≈ 25s TTFT; at ~64 experts ≈ 3.6s, a 7x cut. Decode gains are less certain—even 60% cache hits drop expert bytes/token from 1.3 GB to ~0.5 GB, lifting I/O-bound decode to ~5-8 tok/s. Cheapest test: on 20 held-out prompts, log unique experts per 500-token prefill and tok/s after one tuning epoch, plus quality delta; keep base router as fallback.

Quantize active experts to 2-bit (mixed 2/3/4-bit): 69GB→~34GB, so all experts fit in 32GB RAM and I/O stops bounding decode. This attacks bytes-per-token, not compute: ~0.6GB/token at 2b vs 1.3GB at 4.3b. With 32GB resident, read rate is irrelevant, leaving the 4.6 tok/s compute cap—so you go from 2-4 tok/s I/O-bound to ~4.6 tok/s, only 1.5-2.3x, NOT 3x. To clear 3x, add k=2 speculative verify in one forward (~1.6x bytes, ~2 accepted tokens per forward), totaling ~3-4x. 2-bit experts cost real accuracy (test perplexity); verify is exact. Pin ~24.5% of expert slices (26GB budget) and bias only the 10-of-512 selection, not weights. Routing ~half of each token's experts from the pinned set cuts I/O from 1.3GB to ~0.65GB/token, giving ~2x headroom toward the 4.6 tok/s compute ceiling—so expect 1.15–2.3x, not 3x; the compute ceiling caps any hit-rate trick. Cheapest test: one 2k-token prompt, sweep bias b∈{0,0.5,1}, log miss bytes/token and perplexity; success = ≥1.8x tok/s at ≤2% perplexity rise.

Expert-major prefill cuts I/O (650GB→~69GB, 271s→29s) but compute then binds at ~109s (6TFLOP at 55GFLOP/s), only ~2.5x—not 3x. To hit ≤83s you must also cut prefill FLOPs via draft/early-exit or chunked lookahead, which is lossy; expert-major GEMM itself is exact. First measure per-layer expert histogram over the 500-token prompt to verify coverage and real byte count.

Pin a per-prompt hot set learned during prefill, not shipped offline: after prefill keep the ~24GB of expert slices it loaded in RAM, evicting only cold ones. Same-prompt reuse is 35-42%, so assume 40%: bytes/token 1.3GB→0.78GB, at 2.4GB/s≈3 tok/s; with 42% prev-token repeat and 0.55 layer-prediction prefetch, effective misses fall further, but compute caps at 4.6 tok/s. Realistic gain ~2x, not 3x; the 3x needs striping two NVMes (4.8GB/s) so I/O stops binding and compute becomes the wall. Cheapest measurement: log prefill-loaded expert hit-rate over one prompt's decode; if >40%, build it.

TTFT is I/O/amortisation-bound, so attack prefill bytes, not decode FLOPs. During prefill, cap each layer to top-4 gate experts per token instead of 10 (dynamic top-k). Bytes per token: 48 layers×4 experts×0.9 MB×3 tensors≈0.52 GB vs 1.3 GB at k=10, a 2.5x cut; at 2.4 GB/s a 500-token prefill drops from ~29 s toward ~11 s, decode rises ~2.5x toward 5-10 tok/s. Quality cost: a few benchmark points. Cheapest test: one 500-token prefill at k=4 vs k=10, timing TTFT and bytes read.

Put a small GPU in front as a resident expert cache that also adds FLOPS: ~1.9 GB dense plus ~20 GB hot experts. At 42% same-prompt reuse, ~278 of 480 slices miss: 278×0.9 MB ≈ 0.25 GB/token, not 0.75; at 1.56 GB/s that's ~0.16 s/token ≈ 6.2 tok/s, overlapped with GPU compute. But verify real tok/s—at batch 1 a GEMV is memory-bound, so don't assume 2000 GFLOP/s beats the CPU's 12 GFLOP/token ceiling. Cheapest first measurement: same-prompt expert hit rate at 20 GB cache on your own prompts.

Prefill is compute-bound (500×12 GFLOP=6 TFLOP; ~109s TTFT at 55 GFLOP/s), so attack that ceiling, not decode. Top-10→top-4 gives ~1.8-2.2x, not 2.5x, since dense/attention FLOPs are fixed—measure, don't assume. Moving dense+attention to GPU helps, but expert slices still cross PCIe, so prefill stays host-bound unless hot experts are GPU-resident. Realistic combined gain ~2-3x, not 5x; cost is +0.3-0.8 perplexity.

AVX512-VNNI (zmm vpdpbusd) Q4_K and Q6_K expert dot kernels for decode - Add an AVX512BW/VNNI path for ggml_vec_dot_q4_K_q8_K and q6_K_q8_K (and the MUL_MAT_ID call path). Use vpdpbusd per 32-weight sub-block into int32 lanes, apply the 6-bit scales and mins after the dot, and keep the AVX2 path as fallback. Output must stay near-identical; integer sums are exact, so identity tests should pass.

Overlap expert reads with compute using blocking I/O threads and hits-first ordering - Issue the miss preads for a layer as soon as the router output is known, from 2 dedicated blocking threads (not part of the ggml spin pool), and compute cache-hit experts first so miss compute starts when data lands. Optionally pipeline the next layer's reads with a lossless same-layer-only ordering. No prediction is needed for the hits-first part.

Barrier cost: poll level, thread priority/QoS and straggler sensitivity of the ggml threadpool - Test llama.cpp's own --poll (0-100), --prio (0-3) and cpu-strict options; on macOS also set thread QoS to USER_INTERACTIVE and a thread-affinity tag. Longer term: hybrid spin-then-block barrier (spin about 50 us, then os_sync_wait_on_address or ulock) so a straggler does not burn the sibling hyperthread.

The pool then issues one pread per miss, 4 in flight.

Fetch every miss in the top slots. On average 0.58 of 8 experts per layer are dropped (vs 2 for top-6), so the dropped gate mass is roughly 29% of what top-6 drops.

Decayed-frequency eviction plus routing-replay lookahead (layer-phase aware) in the expert pool - Replace pool LRU with priority = decayed per-key use count (half-life ~16 tokens, lazy heap, ~40 lines), evict lowest priority not used by the current token, ties by recency; optionally protect keys appearing in the tokens that followed the best-matching earlier routing context (suffix-match over the last 2 tokens' expert sets, like prompt-lookup but on routing).

Can be combined with idea 1 as a cheap fallback predictor.

Cache entries carry their precision and an LHU-style upgrade rule.

Falls back to the full head when the margin is too small.

Decode happens once per miss and the cache holds decoded pages.

Defer the missed experts' contribution by one layer (disk-backed expert deferral) - Treat cache misses like KTransformers treats its deferred experts. Hit experts are computed and added to the residual now. Cache-state-aware deferral: only defer when the read would stall - Make deferral conditional: compute at the layer how long the pending reads will take given queue depth, and defer only the misses that cannot land within the expert window, ranked by lowest router weight and lowest layer sensitivity. A small d_max cap (1 or 2) bounds the quality loss. This combines the deferral idea with the S1 pipeline so that most layers are exact.

Expert-major repack of the GGUF so gate, up and down of one expert are one contiguous extent - Offline: write a second file in which each (layer, expert) stores its three weight blocks back to back, and point the pool's offsets file at it. The pool then needs one pread per miss, and a single I/O thread achieves 2.1 GB/s rather than 1.3. Lossless.

Software-pipeline two independent streams (interleaved layers) so one stream's reads hide behind the other's compute - For agent-style workloads with two or more concurrent sessions (or two speculative branches), run the layers of stream A and B offset by half a layer, so A's expert reads overlap B's attention and expert compute. No prediction, no quality risk, but each stream shares the cache and its own per-token latency does not improve.

Token-boundary read-ahead for the first layers from a token-id to expert table - At the end of token t the next token id is known (greedy). Look up the layer-0..2 expert sets seen previously for that token id (layer 0 routing depends mostly on the embedding) and queue them on the I/O helper while the lm_head and sampler finish.

Pin the non-expert (dense) weights so the pool path stops faulting through mmap - At load, after mapping, mlock (or pread into wired anonymous memory) every tensor that is not a routed-expert tensor (attention, router, shared parts, embeddings and output head, about 1-1.5 GB on Qwen3-30B, a few GB on the 125B), guarded by a memory budget and ulimit -l (currently unlimited; vm.global_user_wire_limit is 13 GB). Optional env switch, default off.

Add a pre-run check in the bench harness that refuses to record A/B pairs when foreign CPU exceeds 10%.

Memory-pressure adaptive pool size (shrink before the OS swaps, grow when free) - Size the pool at startup from vm_stat (free + inactive + purgeable minus a floor), and register a dispatch_source MEMORYPRESSURE (warn/critical) plus a periodic kern.memorystatus_level read (live value 73) to release LRU tail slots instead of letting macOS compress or swap them; grow back when pressure clears. Keep non-expert weights pinned (idea 1) so they never fall victim.

Mac background IO hygiene: exclude model storage from Spotlight and Time Machine, run the process with default IO policy, and keep disk at low queue contention - Before each measurement: mdutil -i off on the model volume or touch .metadata_never_index, tmutil addexclusion for the models folder, caffeinate (already on), confirm no Photos/cloud sync via fs_usage -w -f filesys during a 30 s window, and set IO policy IOPOL_IMPORTANT for the reader threads with setiopolicy_np. Compressed or swapped expert tier via the macOS compressor (null test, proposed and killed) - Idea: store evicted experts in compressed RAM so a miss costs a decompress instead of a 0.9 MB SSD read. Test is a pure measurement of compressibility on the weights.

Persistent on-disk KV / prefix cache (save and restore prompt state across turns and sessions) - Hash the token prefix, store KV state to NVMe after the first prefill, and on a match read it back with the explicit pool path (sequential, 3.1 GB/s) and prefill only the new tail. Keep the in-RAM prefix check for within-session turns and add disk persistence for cross-session reuse.

Prefill ubatch sizing plus layer-sequential expert streaming overlapped with batched compute - For prefill only: (a) read each layer's whole expert tensors sequentially with large reads, a layer ahead of compute, because the full set is known in advance and no routing prediction is needed; (b) raise the ubatch so reads amortise (1024-2048) and the read is hidden under compute; (c) skip the LRU for prefill reads (stream through a small ring buffer rather than polluting the decode cache).

Needs a retokenisation guard at the boundary.
